## Commentary on the Khandhavagga
## Saṃyutta Nikāya
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Khandhasaṃyutta
## 1. Nakulapituvagga
## 1. Commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta

In the first sutta of the Khandhiyavagga (the Nakulapitu Sutta), "among the Bhaggas" (*bhaggesu*) refers to the country of that name. "At Susumāragira" (*susumāragire*) refers to the city of Susumāragira. It is said that while that city was being built, a crocodile made a sound; because of that, they named the city "Susumāragira." "In the Bhesakaḷā Forest" (*bhesakaḷāvane*) refers to the forest that received this name because a demoness named Bhesakaḷā resided there. That same forest is called the "Deer Park" (*migadāya*) because it was given as a sanctuary for herds of deer. The Blessed One, relying on that city in that country, dwelt in that forest grove. "Nakulapitā" means the father of a boy named Nakula.

"Old" (*jiṇṇa*) means worn out by decay. "Aged" (*vuḍḍha*) means advanced in years. "Elderly" (*mahallaka*) means one who is senior in days since birth. "Gone past the stages" (*addhagata*) means having reached the end (of the three stages of life). "Reached the final age" (*vayo-anuppatta*) means having reached the last of those three stages of life. "Afflicted in body" (*āturakāya*) means having a diseased body. For this body, even if it is golden-colored, is indeed "afflicted" in the sense of constantly oozing.
230:
Indeed, specifically for that householder, there are three kinds of affliction: affliction by decay, affliction by disease, and affliction by death. Among these, although this householder is afflicted by decay because of his old age, here "afflicted by disease" is intended because of his constant illness. "Afflicted by frequent ailments" (*abhikkhaṇātaṅko*) means having a constant disease, an incessant disease. "Seeing infrequently" (*aniccadassāvī*) means that because of such illness, he is unable to come for an audience at every desired moment, and only occasionally gets the chance to see [the Buddha]; the meaning is "not at all times." "Those who are mind-developing" (*manobhāvanīyānaṃ*) refers to those who cause the wholesome mind to grow. For when such Great Elders as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna are seen, the mind grows by way of wholesome states; those Great Elders are called "mind-developing." "May he instruct" (*anusāsatu*) means may he advise repeatedly. For the first speech is called "exhortation" (*ovāda*), and repeated advice is called "instruction" (*anusāsanī*). Alternatively, speech given when a matter has arisen is called "exhortation," while that spoken before a matter arises, by way of the Pali texts or by way of tradition, is called "instruction." In another way, "exhortation" and "instruction" are the same in meaning, differing only in phrasing.

"This afflicted one" (*āturo hāyaṃ*) means this body is indeed afflicted; even if it is golden-colored or dark-yellow like a *piyaṅgu* fruit, it is afflicted in the sense of constantly oozing. "Become like an egg" (*aṇḍabhūto*) means one who is weak like an egg. Just as a hen's egg or a peacock's egg cannot be played with by catching and throwing or hitting it like a ball—it breaks right then—so too this body breaks if it stumbles on thorns or stumps; thus it is "become like an egg." "Enveloped" (*pariyonaddho*) means enveloped by a mere delicate skin. For an egg is enveloped by a hard shell; therefore, even if mosquitoes, gnats, and the like land on it, they cannot pierce the shell to make the fluid ooze out. But in this body, they can pierce the skin and do as they wish. Thus it is enveloped by a delicate skin. "What else but foolishness" (*kimanyatra bālyā*) means what else is there besides the state of being a fool? The meaning is "this person is just a fool." "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because this body is of such a nature.

"He approached him" (*tenupasaṅkami*): like a royal servant who, after attending upon a Wheel-turning King, goes to attend upon the Crown Prince immediately after, he approached the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to pay respects to the General of Dhamma immediately after attending upon the Blessed One, the Wheel-turning King of the True Dhamma. "Very serene" (*vippasannāni*) means exceptionally clear. "Faculties" (*indriyāni*) means the faculties with the mind as the sixth. "Pure" (*parisuddho*) means faultless.
231:
Pariyodāto is just a synonym for the word parisuddho (pure). It is called "completely pure" because it is free from the defilements of impurities, not because of a white color. Just by seeing the purity of that householder, [the Buddha] knew the clarity of his sense faculties. It is said that this knowledge is the Elder's "knowledge of grasping the method" (nayaggāha-paññā).

"How could it not be obtained? (Kathañhi no siyā)" means for what reason would it not be obtained? It will certainly be obtained. By this statement, the state of intimacy with the Teacher is shown. It is said that from the time this householder saw the Teacher, he felt a fatherly love, and the female householder felt a motherly love. Both of them called the Teacher "my son." This is because they had a love that followed from a previous life. It is said that for five hundred births, that female lay follower was the Buddha's own mother, and that householder was his own father. Again, for five hundred births, the female lay follower was his elder mother (aunt) and the male lay follower was his elder father (uncle). Similarly, for five hundred births, they were his younger mother and younger father. Thus, the Buddha grew up in their hands for one thousand five hundred births.

For that very reason, they would sit in the presence of the Teacher and say things they would not dare to say even in the presence of a son or a father. Because of this, the Blessed One placed these two in the foremost positions (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my lay disciples who are intimate, Nakulapitā the householder is the foremost; Nakulamātā the housewife is the foremost." Wishing to show his intimacy, the householder said, "How could it not be?"

"Anointed with the deathless (Amatena abhisitto)"—in this context, it should not be understood as referring to any particular jhāna, vipassanā, path, or fruit, but rather the sweet teaching of the Dhamma should be known as the "anointing with the deathless" (amatābhiseka). "Even from afar (Dūratopi)" means from another country or another province.

"The uninstructed worldling (Assutavā puthujjanō)" is as explained above. In the words "one who does not see the Noble Ones (Ariyānaṃ adassāvī)," etc., "Noble Ones" (Ariyas) refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, because they are far from defilements, because they do not practice what is harmful (anaya) but only what is beneficial (aya), and because they are worthy of being resorted to by the world including the devas. Or, in this context, only the Buddhas are meant by "Ariyas." As the Blessed One said: "Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called a Noble One." In the term "of the good persons (Sappurisānaṃ)," Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha should be understood as good persons. They are called good persons (sappurisa) because they are beautiful men endowed with supramundane qualities. Alternatively, all of them can be called by both names. Buddhas are both Ariyas and Sappurisas; so are Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. As the Blessed One said:
232:
'One who is grateful and appreciative, wise,
Has good friends and is firm in devotion,
Who respectfully performs the duties for one in distress,
Such a one is called a good person (sappurisa).'

By the words 'Has good friends and is firm in devotion,' a disciple of the Buddha (Buddhasāvaka) is meant. By terms such as gratitude, Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas are meant. Now, one who does not have the habit of seeing those Noble Ones, and does not show respect when seeing them, should be known as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones' (ariyānaṃ adassāvī). This 'not seeing' is of two kinds: not seeing with the eye and not seeing with wisdom. Here, not seeing with wisdom is intended. Indeed, even if Noble Ones are seen with the physical eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) or the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), it is not called 'seeing.' This is because those eyes can only grasp the appearance of color and cannot grasp the state of being a Noble One (ariyahāva). Even domestic dogs, jackals, etc., see Noble Ones with their eyes, but they are not called 'seers of Noble Ones.'

In this regard, there is this story: An elderly monk, who was an attendant to a great Arahant Elder living on Cittalapabbata, was walking for alms with the Elder one day. While carrying the Elder's bowl and robe and following behind him, he asked, 'Venerable Sir, what are Noble Ones like?' The Elder replied, 'Friend, in this Dispensation, some elderly monk might carry the bowl and robe of Noble Ones, perform all the major and minor duties, and travel together with them, yet he does not know the Noble Ones. Friend, Noble Ones are thus difficult to know.' Even when told this, the elderly monk did not understand. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing; only seeing with wisdom is true seeing. As the Blessed One said: 'Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me; he who sees me sees the Dhamma.' Therefore, even if one sees with the eye, if one does not see with wisdom the characteristics such as impermanence (anicca) seen by the Noble Ones, does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, and does not see the qualities that make one a Noble One and the state of being a Noble One, he should be known as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones.'

'Unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones' means being unskillful in the Noble Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). In the phrase 'undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones':

'Discipline (vinaya) is of two kinds, and each of these is fivefold; because of the absence of that discipline, this person is called undisciplined.'
233:
This discipline is of two kinds: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandoning (pahāna-vinaya). Within these two kinds of discipline, each is further divided into five. The discipline of restraint consists of five types: restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara). The discipline of abandoning also consists of five types: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by deliverance (nissaraṇa-pahāna).

Among those disciplines, the restraint described as 'He is endowed, fully endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint' is called restraint by virtue. The restraint described as 'He guards the eye faculty, he practices restraint in the eye faculty' is called restraint by mindfulness. The restraint spoken of by the Blessed One as: 'Whatever streams there are in the world, (O Ajita, said the Blessed One), mindfulness is their obstruction; I declare the restraint of the streams, they are closed by wisdom' is called restraint by knowledge. The restraint described as 'He is one who endures cold and heat' is called restraint by patience. The restraint described as 'He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought' is called restraint by energy.

All this restraint is called 'saṃvara' because it restrains and closes off bodily misconduct and so forth, which ought to be restrained and disciplined, and it is called 'vinaya' because it disciplines and removes them. Thus, first, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint is divided into five. Furthermore, among the insight knowledges such as the discernment of mentality and materiality, there is the abandoning of various unwholesome states that cause harm by means of each respective insight knowledge, because they are opposites, just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp. These abandonings are as follows: abandoning the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) by the knowledge that defines mentality and materiality; abandoning the view of no-cause (ahetu-diṭṭhi) and the view of wrong-cause (visama-hetu-diṭṭhi) by the knowledge that discerns the causes; abandoning the state of doubt by the knowledge of overcoming doubt which occurs subsequent to that; abandoning the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' by the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa); abandoning the perception of the path in what is not the path by the knowledge of defining the path and non-path; abandoning the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by the knowledge of seeing the arising; abandoning the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) by the knowledge of seeing the passing away; abandoning the perception of safety in the five aggregates which are fearful by the knowledge of seeing terror; abandoning the perception of gratification by the knowledge of seeing danger; by the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment...
234:
...abandoning the perception of delight by the knowledge of disenchantment; abandoning the desire not to be delivered by the knowledge of desire for deliverance; abandoning non-equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity towards formations; abandoning those views (eternalism and annihilationism) which are contrary to the status of phenomena (paṭiccasamuppāda) and Nibbāna by the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa); and abandoning the grasping of the sign of formations by the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa)—this is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna).

Furthermore, the abandoning of various hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth by means of concentration, categorized as access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), because it prevents the occurrence of defilements—just as moss on the surface of water is pushed away by hitting it with a pot—is called abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). The abandoning of the group of defilements belonging to the side of the origin (samudaya-sacca) in one's own continuity by means of the four Noble Paths that have been developed, in the manner stated as 'for the abandoning of views' and so forth, so that they never occur again, is called abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). The subsiding of defilements at the moment of Fruition (phala) is called abandoning by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna).

Nibbāna, which is the escape from all conditioned things because it is free from all conditioned things, is called abandoning by deliverance (nissaraṇa-pahāna). All this abandoning is called 'pahāna' in the sense of giving up, and 'vinaya' in the sense of absolute destruction; therefore, it is called 'the discipline of abandoning' (pahāna-vinaya). Alternatively, it is called 'the discipline of abandoning' because such discipline occurs in a person who possesses those respective abandonings. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of abandoning is also divided into five.

In this way, this discipline, which is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail, does not exist in an unlearned worldling (puthujjana) because his restraint is broken and the unwholesome states to be abandoned have not yet been abandoned. Because of the absence of that discipline, such a worldling is called 'untrained' (avinīta). In the context of 'one who has not seen the virtuous ones, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the virtuous ones, who is untrained in the Dhamma of the virtuous ones,' it should be understood in this same way. In terms of meaning, there is no difference between these two. As it is said: 'Those who are Noble Ones (ariyas) are themselves the Virtuous Ones (sappurisas). Those who are Virtuous Ones are themselves the Noble Ones. That which is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones is itself the Dhamma of the Virtuous Ones. That which is the Dhamma of the Virtuous Ones is itself the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. Those which are the disciplines (vinaya) of the Noble Ones are themselves the disciplines of the Virtuous Ones. Those which...'
235:
The discipline of the good persons (sappurisa-vinaya) is also the same as the discipline of the noble ones (ariya-vinaya). Whether it is called the discipline of the noble ones, the discipline of the good persons, the Dhamma of the noble ones, the Dhamma of the good persons, the Vinaya of the noble ones, or the Vinaya of the good persons, these terms have the same meaning, are identical, share the same nature, and originate from the same source. Those noble ones are indeed the good persons. The noble ones also possess the nature of the good persons. They are one and the same without distinction.

Regarding the phrase 'regards form as self' (rūpaṃ attato samanupassati): in this world, a certain person repeatedly regards form as self. He regards form and self as one and the same, thinking, 'Whatever form there is, that is I; whatever I am, that is form.' For example, just as when an oil lamp is burning, the flame is the color and the color is the flame, regarding the flame and the color as one without distinction, so too does one regard form as self. In this way, one regards form as 'self' through the insight of wrong view (diṭṭhi-passanā). Alternatively, one regards self as possessing form. Taking the mental (nāma) as 'self,' one regards that self as possessing form, like a tree possessing a shadow. Or one regards form as being in the self. Taking the mental alone as 'self,' one regards form as being in the self, like a scent in a flower. Or one regards self as being in form. Taking the mental alone as 'self,' one regards that self as being in form, like a gem in a casket. 'Pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī' means standing in a state of obsession or overwhelming. It refers to one who takes hold of form by swallowing it with craving and wrong view, thinking, 'I am form, form is mine.' For such a person, the form thus grasped is called 'tassa taṃ rūpaṃ.' The same method should be understood for the aggregates of feeling (vedanā) and so on.

In that Pali text, in the first point 'regards form as self,' only pure form is taught as self. In the seven instances—'self as possessing form, form in self, self in form, regarding feeling as self... perception... mental formations... consciousness as self'—the mental (nāma) is taught as self. In the twelve instances—by way of three for each of the four mental aggregates, such as 'self as possessing feeling, feeling in self, self in feeling'—a self consisting of a mixture of form and the mental is taught. Among these twenty instances, in the five instances of 'regarding form as self, feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness as self,' the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is taught. In the remaining fifteen instances, the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) is taught. Thus, there are fifteen views of existence (eternalism) and five views of non-existence (annihilationism). All these views obstruct the Path (magga-āvaraṇa), but they do not obstruct heaven (sagga-āvaraṇa). It should be understood that they are abandoned by the first Path (Sotāpatti-magga).

In the passage 'Thus, householder, one is afflicted in body and afflicted in mind,' the physical body (rūpa-kāya) is indeed subject to affliction even for the Buddhas. However, the mind is said to be 'afflicted' when it is followed by lust and so on. In this sutta, the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, shows the mind as being afflicted in this manner. He also shows the state of the mind being unafflicted due to the absence of defilements. By this method, it is shown in this sutta that worldlings (puthujjana) have both an afflicted body and an afflicted mind. Arahants, though they have an afflicted body, have a mind free from affliction. The seven types of trainees (sekha) have minds free from affliction regarding the defilements they have abandoned, but have afflicted minds regarding the defilements they have not yet abandoned.
236:
Regarding the statement, 'Thus, householder, one is both afflicted in body and afflicted in mind,' the body is indeed afflicted even for the Buddhas. However, a mind followed by lust, hatred, and delusion is called an 'afflicted mind,' and that is what is shown here. 'Not afflicted in mind' refers to the state of the mind being unafflicted due to the absence of defilements. Thus, in this sutta, it is shown that the worldly masses are both afflicted in body and afflicted in mind; Arahants (khīṇāsava) are afflicted in body but unafflicted in mind; and the seven trainees (sekha) are neither entirely unafflicted in mind nor entirely afflicted in mind. However, they mostly associate with the state of being unafflicted in mind (unlike worldlings). The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Devadaha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, the Devadaha Sutta, 'Devadaha' is so called because kings are called 'devas,' and it refers to either the auspicious pond (daha) of those kings or a pond that arose spontaneously. The market town (nigama) near that pond is also known as 'Devadaha' using the neuter gender. 'Pacchābhūmagamikā' refers to those who wish to go to the districts situated in the western region. 'Nivāsanti' means staying for the three-month rains retreat (vassa). 'Apalokito' means having asked for permission; 'apaloketha' means 'you all should ask for permission.' Why did the Blessed One have them ask the Elder for permission? It was because He wished to make them 'those with a burden' (sabhāra—meaning those who are responsible and respectful). For one who lives in the same monastery but does not go to see the senior monk, and departs without asking for permission, is called 'one without a burden' (nibbāra). One who lives in the same monastery, comes to see the senior, and asks for permission when departing, is called 'one with a burden' (sabhāra). The Blessed One had them ask for permission because He thought, 'If these monks become those with a burden in this way, they will grow in virtue and other qualities.'

'Paṇḍito' (wise) means being endowed with the fourfold wisdom, such as skill in the elements (dhātu-kosalla). 'Anuggāhaka' (supportive) means one who supports through both material support (āmisa-anuggaha) and Dhamma support (dhamma-anuggaha). It is said that the Elder Sāriputta, unlike other monks, would not go for alms early in the morning. Instead, after all the monks had left, he would wander through the entire monastery (saṅghārāma), sweeping places that had not been swept, disposing of trash that had not been thrown out, and tidying up beds, stools, wooden utensils, and earthenware that were improperly placed. Why? With the intention: 'Lest wanderers of other sects (aññatitthiya) entering the monastery see it and hold us in contempt.' Then, he would go to the infirmary (gilānasālā), comfort the sick monks, and ask, 'What do you need?' and provide whatever was needed...
237:
For the sake of those sick monks, he would take their young novice disciples and, either through the duty of alms-gathering or in a suitable place, search for medicines. Having given the medicines to those sick monks, he would send the novices back, saying, "The care of the sick is praised by the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. Go, virtuous ones, and be diligent." He himself would then wander for alms, finish his meal at a supporter's house, and only then return to the monastery. This was his regular practice at his permanent residence.

However, when the Blessed One was traveling on a journey, he did not walk ahead wearing sandals and holding a parasol, thinking, "I am the Chief Disciple." Instead, he would take care of those who were elderly, sick, or very young novices on that journey, anointing their painful areas with oil. He would have his own young novices carry their bowls and robes, and he would travel only after taking those monks along, either on that same day or the next. One day, the Teacher saw that Elder [Sāriputta] had arrived very late and, not finding a lodging, was staying in the robe-tent. The next day, the Teacher convened the Sangha of monks, told the story of the elephant, the monkey, and the partridge, and prescribed the training rule: "Lodgings should be assigned according to seniority." In this way, he first supported them with material things. When admonishing, he would admonish a person a hundred or even a thousand times until that person was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Only then would he let them go and admonish another. Those who reached the Fruit of Arahantship by standing in the admonition of that Elder, who taught in this manner, are beyond counting. In this way, he supported them with the Dhamma.

"Passassosuṃ" means those monks did not remain silent, thinking, "He is neither our preceptor, nor our teacher, nor a close acquaintance; what shall we do in his presence?" Instead, they accepted the Teacher's words, saying, "Yes, Bhante." "Eḷagalagumbe" means in a thicket-bower. It is said that the Eḷagala thicket grew in a place with constant water. Then, they made a bower with four posts and placed that thicket on top of it, so that the thicket covered the bower like a roof. After that, they arranged bricks underneath, scattered sand, and prepared a seat. It was a cool daytime resting place where the water-breeze blew. The Elder stayed in that bower. It is in reference to this that "Eḷagalagumbe" is said.

"Nānāverajjagataṃ" means having gone to various foreign kingdoms within the realm of a single king. "Virajja" means a foreign kingdom. Just as a place other than one's own country is called "videsa", a kingdom other than the one where one resides is called "virajja". It is also called "vera". "Khattiyapaṇḍitā" refers to wise kings such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala. "Brāhmaṇapaṇḍitā" refers to wise brahmins such as the brahmin Caṅkī and the brahmin Tārukkha. "Gahapatipaṇḍitā" refers to wise householders such as Citta the householder and Sudatta the merchant. "Samaṇapaṇḍitā" refers to wise wanderers such as Sabhiya and Pilotika. "Vīmaṃsakā" are those who are habituated to searching for meaning. "Kiṃvādī" is an inquiry into one's own doctrine, meaning "What doctrine does the teacher of the venerable ones hold?" "Kimakkhāyī" means asking what kind of advice and instruction he repeatedly teaches to his disciples. Of the Dhamma...
238:
A kingdom other than the one where one habitually resides is called "virajja"; that same "virajja" is called "verajja". "Khattiyapaṇḍitā" are wise kings such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala. "Brāhmaṇapaṇḍitā" are wise brahmins such as the brahmin Caṅkī and the brahmin Tārukkha. "Gahapatipaṇḍitā" are wise householders such as Citta the householder and Sudatta the merchant. "Samaṇapaṇḍitā" are wise wanderers such as Sabhiya and Pilotika. "Vīmaṃsakā" are those who are habituated to searching for meaning. "Kiṃvādī" carries the meaning of inquiring, "What does he say is his own view? What kind of doctrine does he have?" "Kimakkhāyī" means what kind of advice and instruction does he proclaim to his disciples. "Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ" refers to the secondary explanation (anubyākaraṇa) that is in accordance with the Dhamma-explanation (byākaraṇa) spoken by the Blessed One. "Sahadhammiko" means being with reason or cause. "Vādānuvāda" is a secondary statement that follows the doctrine spoken by the Blessed One. There is also a reading "vādānupāto", which means following after the Teacher's doctrine; it has the sense of following or pursuing. By this reading as well, it simply illustrates a doctrine that follows [the original].

In the passages beginning with "avigatarāgassa", the meaning should be understood solely by the power of craving (taṇhā). That same craving is called "rāga" because of its lusting, "chanda" because of its desiring, "pema" in the sense of affection, "pipāsā" in the sense of wanting to drink [the object], and "pariḷāha" in the sense of repeatedly burning. Why is the discourse beginning with "Akusale cāvuso dhamme" initiated? It is to show the danger for one who is not free from lust and the benefit for one who is free from lust regarding the five aggregates. In that text, "avighāto" means freedom from suffering, "anupāyāso" means freedom from intense despair, and "apariḷāha" means freedom from burning. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections. The commentary on the second sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Haliddikāni Sutta

In the third sutta, "Avantīsu" means in the Avanti country, known as the Southern Region (Dakkhiṇāpatha). "Kuraraghare" means in the city of that name. "Papāte" means at a precipice that is as if broken off on one side. It means that one side of that mountain was as if cut and dropped, forming a great precipice. There is also a reading "pavatte", which means the place where the doctrines of various sectarians occur. Thus, the Elder Mahākaccāna resided on that mountain with the precipice, depending on the city of Kuraraghara in that Avanti country. "Haliddikāni" is the person of that name. "Aṭṭhakavaggiye Māgaṇḍiyapañhe" means there is a question asked by the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the Octad Chapter; it refers to that question. "Rūpadhātu" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). "Rūpadhāturāgavinibaddhaṃ" means bound by lust for the element of form. "Viññāṇaṃ" refers to kamma-viññāṇa (karmic consciousness). "Okasārī" means one who habitually dwells in a home, one who is attached by the power of craving and views.
239:
Householder, why is 'viññāṇadhātu' (element of consciousness) not mentioned here? It is to dispel confusion. 'Oka' (home) refers to 'cause' in its meaning. Kamma-consciousness that arose previously serves as a condition for subsequent kamma-consciousness and resultant consciousness. Resultant consciousness also serves as a condition for resultant consciousness and kamma-consciousness. If so, confusion might arise as to 'which consciousness is meant here?' To dispel that confusion, this discourse was taught without including that consciousness, keeping it unmixed. Alternatively, consciousness is not included here to show the four stations of volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) by way of the object.

'Upayupādāna' refers to the two 'upaya' (approaches)—craving and view—and the four 'upādāna' (clinging), such as clinging to sensual pleasures. 'Cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusaya' refers to those states which are the standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies of the unwholesome mind. 'Tathāgata' refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. Although these states are abandoned by all Arahants, the Buddha's state of being one whose taints are destroyed is extremely well-known in the world; thus, it is stated in terms of the highest limit. In the phrase 'viññāṇadhātu', why is consciousness included here? It is to show the abandonment of defilements. Defilements are not only abandoned in the four aggregates but are abandoned in all five aggregates; thus, consciousness is included to show the abandonment of defilements. Householder, in this way, one who does not frequent the 'oka' (home)—the five aggregates—by way of kamma-consciousness is called 'anokasārī' (one who wanders without a home).

'Rūpanimittaniketanisāravinibandha': Form itself is called 'nimitta' (sign) because it is a cause for defilements. It is called 'niketa' (abode) because it is a place of dwelling known as making an object. Therefore, form itself is both the sign and the abode. By the two terms 'visāra' (spreading) and 'vinibandha' (bond), the spreading and binding nature of defilements is meant. Thus, it means the spreading and binding of defilements that arise in the temporary abode of form. One who frequents the temporary abode by way of making an object is called 'niketasārī' (one who wanders in an abode). The spreading and binding of defilements in that temporary abode of form have been abandoned.

Why are the five aggregates called 'oka' (permanent home) and the six objects called 'niketa' (temporary abode) here? It is because of the strength or weakness of desire and lust (chandarāga). Although the five aggregates and six objects are similar in the sense of being a dwelling place, in the world, only a permanent dwelling place is called 'oka'. Places like gardens where one stays momentarily, having made an appointment saying 'Let us play in such a place today,' are called 'niketa'. Just as desire and lust are strong in a house filled with wife, children, wealth, and grain, so too they are strong in the internal five aggregates...
240:
'Niketa' refers to a temporary dwelling place such as a garden, a place designated by an agreement like 'Let us play in such and such a place today.' Just as desire and lust (chandarāga) are strong for a house filled with wife, children, wealth, and grain, so too desire and lust are strong for the internal five aggregates. Just as desire and lust are weaker in places like gardens than in a house, so too desire and lust are weak for the six external objects. It should be understood that this discourse was taught by way of the strength and weakness of desire and lust.

'Sukhitesu sukhito' (happy among the happy) means when the supporting lay followers are happy due to wealth, grain, gains, etc., one feels happy with the happiness of a householder based on craving, thinking, 'Now I will receive agreeable food and snacks.' It is living as if experiencing the prosperity attained by those lay followers oneself. 'Dukkhitesu dukkhito' (sad among the sad) means when those lay followers encounter suffering for some reason, one feels sad with double the suffering oneself. 'Kiccakarāṇīyesu' refers to various duties and obligations. In those matters, 'yogam āpajjati' means personally exerting great effort to perform the tasks of those lay followers. 'Kāmesu' refers to objective sensuality (vatthukāma). When the Buddha said, 'Householder, in this way one is not empty of sensual pleasures,' it means not being empty of the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma), and not being void because of the presence of sensuality within one's own continuity. On the bright side (sukkapakkha), it should be understood that one is empty or void because of the absence of those sensual pleasures.

'Purakkharāno' means one who puts the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) in front and prioritizes it. It is the wishing and longing for forms such as long, short, black, or white, saying, 'May I have such a form.' Likewise, in feelings (vedanā) such as pleasure, in perceptions (saññā) such as the perception of blue, in volitional formations (saṅkhāra) such as meritorious formations, and in consciousness (viññāṇa) such as eye-consciousness, one wishes and longs, 'May I have such feelings, perceptions, volitional formations, and consciousness.'

'Apurakkharāno' means one who does not put the round of rebirth in front. In the phrase 'My speech is consistent, your speech is inconsistent (not connected),' it means your speech is not smooth, while my speech is very smooth, like a sweet drink (madhurapāna). 'The doctrine you have long practiced is overturned' means the speech you have practiced and mastered over a long time has retreated and changed in an instant upon meeting my doctrine. 'A charge (fault) has been placed on you' means I have exposed and presented the fault that exists in you. 'Wander for the release from the doctrine' means approach various teachers, seek higher knowledge, and wander while striving to be released from this charge that has been placed. 'Or if you are able, explain it right here' means if you are personally capable, then answer and clarify it right here. The third (Nakulapitu Sutta) is finished.
241:
## 4. Commentary on the Second Hāliddikāni Sutta
In the fourth sutta, 'Sakkapañha' refers to what was spoken in the Cūḷasakkapañha Sutta and the Mahāsakkapañha Sutta. 'Taṇhākkhayavimutta' means liberated by fruition-liberation (phalavimutti) having Nibbāna—the destruction of craving—as its object. 'Accantaniṭṭhā' means the finality that transcends the end, an eternal completion. The same method applies to the remaining terms. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta
In the fifth sutta, the Blessed One gave this teaching on 'concentration' (samādhi) seeing those monks declining in one-pointedness of mind. Knowing that 'if these monks attain one-pointedness of mind, their meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) will flourish,' he spoke it. "Abhinandati" means to yearn for. "Abhivadati" means to say, through that delight, "Oh, how dear, desirable, pleasant, and agreeable!" Even one who speaks words of praise, by depending on that object and thus giving rise to greed, is said to "welcome" (abhivadati). "Ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati" means to swallow and hold on firmly. "Delight in form (nandī)" is the delight known as strong yearning for form. "Clinging to that (upādāna)" is called clinging (upādāna) because of the sense of firm grasping. "Does not delight (nābhinandati)" means does not yearn for. "Does not welcome (nābhivadati)" means not saying "desirable, pleasant" by way of yearning. Even if one utters "impermanent, suffering" with a mind of insight, it is not "welcoming" (with craving). The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Paṭisallāṇa Sutta
In the sixth sutta, the Blessed One gave this teaching on 'seclusion' (paṭisallāṇa) seeing those monks declining in physical seclusion (kāyaviveka). Knowing that 'if these monks attain physical seclusion, their meditation subject will flourish,' he spoke it. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Upādāparitassanā Sutta
In the seventh sutta, "Upādāparitassanā" is the agitation and anxiety arising from grasping. "Anupādāaparitassanā" is the absence of agitation due to non-grasping. "Consciousness follows the change of form" means that kamma-consciousness follows the destruction of form in such ways as "My form has changed" or "This was mine, but now it is not." "Arising from following the change" means because of following the change...
242:
...born from a mind that has change as its object. "Arising of the states of agitation" (paritassanā dhammasamuppāda) refers to the agitation of craving and the arising of unwholesome states other than craving. "Mind" (citta) refers to the wholesome mind. "They stand having exhausted" (pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti) means they stand having exhausted the wholesome mind, not giving it an opportunity to arise. "Fearful" (uttāsavā) means having fear by being established in craving. "Distressed" (vighātavā) means having distress along with suffering. "Longing" (apekkhavā) means having yearning (ālayo). "Grasping, he is agitated" (upādāya ca paritassati) means one who, having grasped with craving and views, becomes agitated by the power of craving. "Does not follow the change of form" means that for an Arahant, kamma-consciousness itself does not exist; therefore, it should be said in every respect that there is no following the destruction of form. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Second Upādāparitassanā Sutta
In the eighth sutta, the teaching is given by way of craving, conceit, and views. Thus, in these four suttas in succession, only the round of suffering and the cessation of the round (vaṭṭavivaṭṭa) are spoken of. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Kālattayaanicca Sutta
In the ninth sutta, "What need is there to speak of the present form?" means that the present form is certainly impermanent. It is said that those monks, while noting the past and future as impermanent, were struggling with the present. Then the Teacher, knowing their disposition, taught this discourse according to the individual's inclination, thinking, "If the present is spoken of as impermanent even more than the past and future, they will understand." The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10-11. Commentary on the Kālattayadukkha Sutta, etc.
10-11. The tenth and eleventh suttas are spoken according to the disposition of such individuals, distinguishing them with the terms 'suffering' (dukkha) and 'non-self' (anattā). The tenth and eleventh suttas are finished.

## 1-10. Commentary on the Anicca Sutta, etc.
12-21. In the Anicca Chapter, the final sutta is according to the request of the Venerable Ānanda, while the remaining suttas are taught according to the power of those individuals who would understand in various ways. The first sutta and the others are finished.

## 3. The Burden Group (Bhāravagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Burden Discourse (Bhārasutta-vaṇṇanā)
In the first sutta of the Bhāravagga, the words "the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā)" are spoken. It means it should be said thus: the five aggregates which are the objects of clinging. "Monks, this is called the burden"—those which are these five aggregates of clinging, these are called the heavy burden. In what sense is it called a burden? In the sense of the extreme heaviness of maintenance. The maintenance of these five aggregates of clinging—such as making them stand, walk, sit, lie down, bathing them, adorning them, feeding them, etc.—is a heavy burden that is hard to endure; therefore, it is called a burden in the sense of the heaviness of maintenance.

"Having such a name" means having a name such as Tissa or Datta. "Having such a clan" means having a clan such as Kaṇhāyana or Vacchāyana. Thus, [the Buddha] shows the individual, who is established merely by designation, as the "burden-bearer." Indeed, at the very moment of rebirth, the individual takes up the burden of the aggregates and carries this burden of the aggregates for ten years, twenty years, or even a hundred years—throughout life—bathing it, feeding it, making it sit and lie down on soft-to-the-touch couches and chairs, and after discarding it at the moment of death, takes up another new burden of aggregates again at the moment of rebirth. Therefore, he is known as the "burden-bearer" (bhārahāra).

"Leading to renewed existence (Ponobbhavika)" means having the nature of producing rebirth in a new existence. "Accompanied by delight and lust (Nandīrāgasahagata)" means having reached a state of oneness with delight and lust. Here, the state of being together with that delight and lust is intended. "Finding delight here and there (Tatra tatrābhinandinī)" means having the habit of greatly delighting in that particular existence or in objects such as visible forms, whether in the place of rebirth or in sense objects. Among the types of craving such as craving for sensual pleasures, lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is called "craving for sensual pleasures" (kāma-taṇhā). Lust for existence in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, lust for jhāna, and lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) is called "craving for existence" (bhava-taṇhā). Lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is called "craving for non-existence" (vibhava-taṇhā).

"Taking up the burden (Bhārādāna)" means the grasping of the burden. This is because this individual takes up the burden through craving. "The fading away and cessation without remainder (Asesavirāganirodha)" and all such words are merely synonyms for Nibbāna. Depending on that Nibbāna, craving fades away without remainder, ceases, is given up, is relinquished, and is released. Since there is no "abode of sensual pleasure" (kāmālaya) or "abode of views" (diṭṭhālaya) in this Nibbāna, Nibbāna receives these names. "Craving with its root (Samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ)" means ignorance (avijjā) is the root of craving. "Having uprooted (Abbuyha)" means having pulled out that craving along with its root by the Path of Arahatship. "Without hunger, cooled (Nicchāto parinibbuto)" means it is proper to say that one is free from craving and the defilements are extinguished. The first sutta is finished.
244:
## 2. Pariññasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "pariññeyya" (to be fully understood) means those things that should be fully understood through full understanding (pariññā), and those things that should be transcended by abandoning craving and lust (chandarāga). "Pariññā" refers to Nibbāna, which is the ultimate full understanding and the ultimate transcendence. The terms beginning with "rāgakkhaya" (destruction of lust) are names for Nibbāna. Indeed, that Nibbāna is called absolute full understanding (accanta-pariññā). The second sutta ends.

## 3. Abhijānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "abhijānaṃ" means knowing with higher knowledge. By this word "abhijānanti," full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) is taught. By the second word "parijānanti," full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) is taught. By the third and fourth words "virajjanti" and "pajahanti," full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) is taught. Thus, in this sutta, the three types of full understanding are taught. The third sutta ends.

## 4-9. Chandarāgasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
25-30. From the fourth sutta to the eleventh sutta, these eight suttas should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Dhātu Saṃyutta. Specifically, in these suttas, the Four Noble Truths are taught in the fifth, sixth, and seventh suttas in sequence, and the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught in the eighth and ninth suttas. The fourth and subsequent suttas end.

## 10. Aghamūlasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "aghaṃ" means suffering (dukkha). Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of suffering is taught. The tenth sutta ends.

## 11. Pabhaṅgusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, "pabhaṅgu" refers to things that have the nature of breaking down at every moment. Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) is taught. The eleventh sutta ends.

## Bhāravaggo Tatiyo.
## 4. Natumhākavaggo
## 1. Natumhākasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Natumhāka Vagga, "pajahatha" means abandon by discarding craving and lust. Among grass (tiṇa) and so forth, "tiṇa" (grass) refers to plants such as palmyra and coconut, which have pith on the inside and are hard on the outside.
245:
"Firewood" (kaṭṭha) refers to types of trees that have heartwood inside and sapwood outside, such as the Cutch tree (khadira), Sal tree (sāla), Teak (sāka), and Jackfruit (panasa). "Branch" (sākhā) refers to the limbs extending from the tree trunk, like arms. "Leaf" (palāsa) refers to leaves such as those of the palmyra palm, coconut palm, and so on. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Natumhāka Sutta
The second sutta is taught according to the inclination of those who can understand without the use of a simile. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Aññatarabhikkhu Sutta
In the third sutta, "Venerable sir, if one has a latent tendency towards form" means if one dwells with a latent tendency by taking form as an object. "By that, one is designated" means among the latent tendencies such as sensual lust, whichever latent tendency dwells taking that form as an object, by that very latent tendency which is currently dwelling, one is designated as "one who is lustful, one who is hateful, one who is deluded." "By that, one is not designated" means one is not designated as "one who is lustful, one who is hateful, one who is deluded" by that latent tendency which has not yet arisen. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Second Aññatarabhikkhu Sutta
In the fourth sutta, "it perishes along with that form" means that the latent tendency perishes along with that form which is its basis. Indeed, when the object-form is breaking up, the states dependent on that object cannot remain. "Along with whichever form it perishes" means whichever form perishes along with whichever latent tendency. "By that, one is designated" means by that latent tendency one is designated as "one who is lustful, one who is hateful, one who is deluded." Alternatively, the word "yaṃ" has the sense of the instrumental case; it means one is designated as "one who is lustful, one who is hateful, one who is deluded" by the latent tendency with which it perishes. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5-6. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta etc.
37-38. In the fifth sutta, "the alteration of that which is present is evident" means the decay (jarā) of that which is existing and living is evident. "Presence" (thiti) is the name for the preservation known as the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). "Alteration" (aññathatta) is a name for decay (jarā). Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
Arising is called birth (jāti), and dissolution is called passing away (vaya).
Alteration is called decay (jarā), and presence (thiti) is preservation.
In this way, for each individual aggregate, there are three characteristics known as arising (uppāda), decay (jarā), and dissolution (bhaṅga). Referring to these three characteristics, it was said: "Monks, these three are the conditioned characteristics of the conditioned" (A. III. 47).
246:
In that (sutta), "conditioned" (saṅkhata) refers to any formation (saṅkhāra) produced by causes. A formation is not the characteristic, and the characteristic is not the formation. It is not possible to make known the characteristic without the formation, nor the formation without the characteristic. However, the formation becomes evident through the characteristic. Just as a cow itself is not the mark, and the mark itself is not the cow; it is not possible to make known the mark apart from the cow, nor the cow apart from the mark. However, by the mark (such as a brand made by a hot iron), this cow becomes evident as belonging to this person; this should be understood in accordance with this simile.

In that context, at the moment of arising of formations, the formation is evident, the characteristic of arising is evident, and the moment of that formation known as time is also evident. Even when "arising" is mentioned, the formation is evident, the characteristic of decay (jarā) is evident, and the moment of decay of that formation known as time is also evident. At the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), the formation is evident, that characteristic of dissolution is evident, and the moment of dissolution of that formation known as time is also evident. Other teachers, however, say: "The moment of decay of immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) cannot be made known." They argue: "Did not the Blessed One, by saying 'the arising of feeling is evident, its passing away is evident, its alteration while present is evident,' show the three characteristics of immaterial phenomena? Those characteristics are obtained by taking the presence (atthikkhana) of immaterial phenomena." Having said this, they establish that meaning with this teacher's verse:

"The presence of all phenomena is called thiti.
The breaking up of that very presence is death for all beings at all times."

Alternatively, they say that "thiti" should be understood as "staying" by way of continuity (santati). However, since there is no such distinction in the Sutta texts, one should not reject the Sutta based on the teachers' opinion (attanomati), but should take the Sutta itself as the authority. The sixth sutta is clear. The fifth and sixth suttas (are finished).

## 7-10. Commentary on the Anudhamma Sutta etc.

39-42. In the seventh sutta, "for one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhamma-paṭipannassa) means for one who practices the preliminary path (pubbabhāgapatipadā) which is the practice in accordance with the nine supramundane states. "This is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (ayam-anudhammo) means what follows is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma. "Full of revulsion" (nibbidā-bahulo) means being full of weariness towards all existences. "Fully understands" (parijānāti) means one fully understands (the phenomena of the three planes) through the three full understandings (pariññā). "Is fully released" (parimuccati) means one is fully released (from all fetters) by the full understanding of abandonment (pahāna-pariññā) occurring at the moment of the path. Thus, in this sutta, only the path is spoken of; likewise in the three suttas following this. In this sutta, however, the contemplation (anupassanā) is not specifically defined...
247:
In these (8th, 9th, and 10th) suttas, the contemplation (anupassanā) is specified. Therefore, in this (7th) sutta as well, that contemplation should be specified exactly as it was in those three suttas. This is because it is not possible to reach weariness (nibbinda) or to fully understand (parijānā) without any one of the three contemplations. The seventh and subsequent suttas are concluded.

## The Fourth Chapter: Natumhāka.

## 5. Attadīpavagga

## 1. Attadīpasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Attadīpavagga, 'attadīpā' means to dwell making oneself an island, a protection, a shelter, a resort, a refuge, and a support. The term 'attasaraṇā' is a synonym for 'attadīpā'. 'Ananyasaraṇā' is a statement rejecting any other refuge. Indeed, one person cannot be the refuge of another because one person's goal cannot be achieved through another's effort. Regarding this, it is said:
'Self is indeed the lord of self; for who else could be the lord?' (Dhammapada 160).
Therefore, it is said 'ananyasaraṇā'. What is meant by 'self' (attā) here? It is the mundane and supramundane Dhamma. For that reason, it is said: 'dhamma-dīpā dhamma-saraṇā ananyasaraṇā'. 'Yoni' means cause, as in 'Bhūmija, this is the cause (yoni) for the attainment of the fruit,' and so on. 'Kiṃpahotikā' means what is the beginning, or from where do they arise? The phrase 'rūpassa tveva' (of form indeed) is begun to show the abandoning of those sorrows and so on. 'Na paritassati' means one does not grasp or cling (with craving). 'Tadaṅganibbuto' means one is 'extinguished by that factor' because the defilements are extinguished by that factor of insight (vipassanā). In this sutta, only insight is discussed. The first sutta is concluded.

## 2. Paṭipadāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, in the passage 'dukkhasamudayagāminī samanupassanā' (contemplation leading to the origin of suffering), because the 'identity' (sakkāya) is suffering, the practice leading to the origin of that suffering is 'repeatedly viewing form as self'.
248:
Thus, contemplation through view (diṭṭhi-samanupassanā) has been taught; therefore, in this sutta, the meaning is 'contemplation leading to the origin of suffering'. In the phrase 'dukkhanirodhagāminī samanupassanā' (contemplation leading to the cessation of suffering), the four path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa) along with insight (vipassanā) are called 'samanupassanā'. Thus, in this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. The second sutta is concluded.

## 3. Aniccasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'sammapaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ' means it should be seen with path-wisdom (magga-paññā) along with insight. 'Virajjati vimuccati' means one becomes dispassionate at the path-moment and is liberated at the fruition-moment. 'Anupādāya āsavehi' means one is liberated in this way without clinging to anything by the taints (āsava) which have ceased through the cessation of non-arising. The words 'rūpadhātuyā' and so on are spoken for the purpose of showing reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Teachers also say it is spoken for the purpose of showing reviewing knowledge along with the fruit. 'Ṭhitaṃ' (standing firm) means standing still because there is no further task to be done above. 'Ṭhitattā santussitaṃ' means being greatly content because the attainment that should be reached has been reached. 'Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyati' means one attains the cooling of defilements by oneself. The third sutta is concluded.

## 4. Dutiya-aniccasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'pubbantānudiṭṭhiyo' means the eighteen views concerning the past do not arise. 'Aparantānudiṭṭhiyo' means the forty-four views concerning the future do not arise. 'Thāmaso parāmāso' means the strong adherence of view and the misapprehension of view do not occur. By this much, the first path is shown. Now, the phrase 'rūpasmiṃ' and so on is begun to show the three paths and fruits along with insight. Alternatively, views are abandoned by insight alone; however, this sutta is begun to show the four paths along with insight above. The fourth sutta is concluded.

## 5. Samanupassanāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'pañcupādānakkhandhe samanupassanti etesaṃ vā aññataraṃ' means one repeatedly contemplates the five aggregates of clinging by way of full grasping, or contemplates one of those aggregates by way of incomplete grasping. 'Iti ayañceva samanupassanā' means 'thus, this is the contemplation of the view of self'. 'Asmīti cassa avigataṃ hoti' means for one who has this contemplation, the three proliferations (papañca)—known as craving, conceit, and view—expressed as 'I am' (asmi), are not removed.
249:
"The descent of the five faculties occurs" means that if the web of defilements—namely craving, conceit, and view—exists, the five faculties arise based on kamma and defilements. The phrase "Monks, there is the mind" refers to the kamma-associated mind (kammamana). "Dhamma" refers to the object of that mind. "Avijjā-dhātu" (the element of ignorance) is the ignorance present at the moment of javana (impulsion). "Avijjā-samphassaja" refers to states arising from contact associated with ignorance. Alternatively, "Mano" (mind) is the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) at the moment of bhavaṅga (life-continuum), and the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) at the moment of āvajjana (adverting). Dhamma and the others are as previously explained. "It also occurs to him, 'I am'" means that through the power of craving, conceit, and view, the thought "I am" occurs to him. Following this, "This is I" is spoken in terms of the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), taking any one of the phenomena such as form (rūpa), etc., and thinking "This is I." "Will be" is through the power of the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). "Will not be" is through the power of the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). All terms such as "will be possessed of form" and so on, lean towards the eternalist view. "Then, in these [faculties]" means in these faculties as they exist in that same manner before the practice of insight. "Ignorance is abandoned" means that ignorance, which is the unknowing of the Four Noble Truths, is abandoned by the arising of the Path through the development of insight. "Knowledge arises" means the arising of the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-vijjā). Thus, in this sutta, craving, conceit, and view, which are called "I am," are termed "kamma" because they are the causes of kamma. There is one connection between kamma and the five faculties; and by including the resultant mind in the side of the five faculties, there is one connection between the five faculties and kamma. In this way, the three proliferations (papañca) belong to the past; the faculties and so on belong to the present. Among those phenomena, starting from the kamma-associated mind, the cause for the future is shown. The fifth sutta is finished.

## ၆။ ခန္ဓသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the sixth sutta, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is a phenomenon of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). The four mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha) occur in the four planes. "Sāsava" (with taints) refers to a phenomenon that is a cause for the taints (āsava) by being their object. "Upādāniya" (clinging-prone) similarly refers to a phenomenon that is a cause for clinging (upādāna) by being its object. The etymological meaning here is: it is called "sāsava" because it occurs together with the taints that arise by making it an object. It is called "upādāniya" because it is to be firmly clung to by the clingings. In these clinging aggregates as well, the aggregate of form is a sense-sphere phenomenon. The remaining four mental aggregates are said to occur in the three planes as the domain of insight. Thus, in this sutta, form is included in the "aggregates" (khandha) in the sense of a heap; it is included in the "clinging aggregates" (upādānakkhandha) in the sense of a heap that is an object of the taints. Regarding feeling and the others, there are those with taints (sāsava) and those without taints (anāsava). All those mental aggregates are included in the "aggregates" in the sense of a heap. Among those mental aggregates, those that occur in the three planes are included in the "clinging aggregates" in the sense of being an object of the taints. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7-8. Soṇasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
49-50. In the seventh sutta, "seyyohamasmī" means "I am superior, I am excellent." "Kimanyatra yathābhūtassa adassanā" means "What other cause could there be besides not seeing things as they really are?" Not seeing means only ignorance (aññāṇa). Now, the Blessed One, wishing to exert the teaching which is like a diamond-wheel (vajira) with three rotations for Soṇa, the householder's son, said "Taṃ kiṃ maññasi Soṇa" and so forth. The eighth sutta is very clear in meaning. The seventh and eighth suttas end.

## 9-10. Nandikkhayasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
51-52. In the ninth and tenth suttas, "nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo" and "rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo" are stated because delight (nandi) and lust (rāga) are not different in meaning. Alternatively, one abandons delight (nandi) by being weary through the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā), and abandons lust (rāga) by being dispassionate through the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā). Having concluded insight (vipassanā) with this much, the Path (magga) is shown by the words "rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo," and the Fruit (phala) is shown by the words "nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ." The ninth and tenth suttas end.
