## 6. Upayavaggo

## 1. Upayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Upaya Vagga, "upayo" refers to one who has approached the five aggregates through the power of craving, conceit, and views. Consciousness (viññāṇa) refers to karmic consciousness (kamma-viññāṇa). "Āpajjeyya" means it would reach growth and so forth, because it is capable of pulling towards rebirth (paṭisandhi) by intensifying kamma. The reason for not including the term "viññāṇupayaṃ" has already been stated. "Vocchijjatarammaṇaṃ" means the object is cut off because of the lack of ability to pull towards rebirth. "Patiṭṭhā viññāṇဿ" means there is no support for karmic consciousness. "Tadappatiṭṭhitaṃ" means that unsupported consciousness. "Anabhisaṅkhacca vimuttaṃ" means liberated without constructing rebirth. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Bījasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "bījazātāni" means seeds. "Mūlabījaṃ" (root-seeds) refers to roots such as orris root, costus, turmeric, ginger, and so forth. "Khandhabījaṃ" (stem-seeds) refers to stem-types such as the Bodhi tree, the banyan tree, and so forth.
251:
Seed from a joint (phalubīja) refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so on. Seed from a top (aggabīja) refers to basil, phanijjaka, and so on. Seed from a seed (bījabīja) refers to initial crops (pubbaṇṇa) such as sāli rice and vīhi rice, and later crops (aparaṇṇa) such as green gram and black gram. Unbroken (akhaṇḍa) means seeds that are not damaged. From the time it is broken, a seed is no longer fit for the purpose of a seed. Not rotten (apūtika) means seeds that are not rotten due to being soaked in water. Indeed, a rotten seed is not fit for the purpose of a seed. Unstruck by wind and sun (avātātapahata) means seeds that are not destroyed by wind and sun, and have not been deprived of their essence. Indeed, a seed that is pithless and mere chaff is not fit for the purpose of a seed. Having essence (sārādāna) means seeds that have acquired essence, in which the essence is established. Indeed, a seed without essence is not fit for the purpose of a seed. Well-rested (sukhasayita) means seeds that have remained well, just as they were placed in a granary for four months. Earth (pathavī) refers to the supporting earth below. Water (āpo) refers to the moisture from above that provides lubrication. The four stations of consciousness (catasso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo) refer to the four aggregates, such as the form aggregate, which are the objects of kamma-consciousness. Because they are the support by way of being objects, they are like the earth element. Delight and lust (nandirāga) is like the water element in the sense of providing moisture. Consciousness with nutriment (viññāṇaṃ sāhāraṃ) refers to kamma-consciousness along with its conditions. That consciousness, like a seed, grows in the earth of the object. The second sutta is finished.

## ၃။ ဥဒါနသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the third sutta, 'he uttered an exclamation' (udānaṃ udānesi) means he gave voice to an exclamation produced by powerful joy (somanassa). On what basis did this exclamation arise for the Blessed One? It arose based on the liberating nature (niyyānikabhāva) of the Dispensation. How so? It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'There are these three supports (upanissaya)—the support of giving (dāna), the support of virtue (sīla), and the support of meditation (ဘာဝနူပနိဿယ).' Among these three, the supports of giving and virtue are weak, while the support of meditation is strong. The supports of giving and virtue lead to the three lower paths and fruits, but the support of meditation leads to Arahatship. Thus, a monk established in a weak support, by striving and exerting, can cut the five lower fetters and produce the three paths and fruits. This exclamation arose for the Blessed One as he reflected, 'Oh, the Dispensation is indeed liberating!'

To clarify this meaning—that 'one established in a weak support, by striving, reaches the three paths and fruits'—the story of Milaka Thera should be understood. It is said that when he was a layman, he made a living by killing living beings, setting a hundred snares and a hundred traps in the forest. One day, after eating roasted meat, while wandering among the snare-sites, he was overcome by thirst and went to the monastery of a forest-dwelling elder. Seeing the water pot standing not far from the elder who was walking in meditation, he opened it. He did not see even enough water to moisten his fingertips. Milaka became angry and said, 'Monks, you eat the good food and curries offered by householders and walk in meditation, yet you do not keep even a handful of water in the water pot. This is not proper!' The elder said, 'I placed the water pot there after filling it,' but that word that there was no water...
252:
He went to the monastery of a forest-dwelling elder and, seeing the water pot standing not far from the elder who was walking in meditation, he opened it, but did not see even enough water to moisten his fingertips. That man became angry and said, 'Monk, monks... you eat and eat the food and snacks offered by householders and then sleep; you do not keep even a handful of water in the water pot. This is not proper.' The elder thought, 'I placed the water pot there after filling it; why does he say this?' and went to look. Seeing the pot full of water, he drew some with a water-conch and gave it to him. After drinking two or three conch-fulls of water, the man thought, 'Even such a full pot of water, because of my kamma, became like a hot potsherd. What will happen in a future existence?' With a mind full of agitation (saṃvega), he threw away his bow and said, 'Venerable sir, please ordain me.' The elder taught him the meditation on the fivefold skin (taca-pañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. 

When he was performing the duties of a recluse, the places where he had killed many deer and pigs, and the places where he had set snares and traps, appeared in his mind. When he remembered those objects, a burning sensation arose in his body, and like a rogue ox, his mind could not enter the path of meditation. He thought, 'What can I do as a monk?' and, oppressed by dissatisfaction, he went to the elder, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, I am unable to perform the duties of a recluse.' Then the elder said, 'Then do some manual work.' He replied, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and cut down moist trees such as the cluster fig (udumbara), made a large pile, and asked, 'What should I do now?' 'Burn it,' the elder said. Although he tried to set it on fire from the four directions, it would not burn, so he said, 'Venerable sir, I cannot.' The elder said, 'In that case, move aside,' and splitting the earth in two, he took out a fire the size of a firefly from the Avīci Hell and threw it into the woodpile. That massive woodpile was incinerated in an instant like dry leaves. Then the elder showed him Avīci Hell and inspired agitation, saying, 'If you return to the lay life, you will be cooked in this hell.' From the time he saw Avīci Hell, he began to tremble and asked, 'Venerable sir, is the Buddha's Dispensation truly a means of escape from the round of suffering?' 'Yes, friend, it is,' the elder replied. 'Venerable sir, if the Buddha's Dispensation is indeed a means of escape, Milaka will work for his own liberation; do not worry,' he said. From then on, he performed the duties of a recluse and strove hard. He fulfilled the major and minor duties for the elder. When overcome by sleepiness, he would place a wet coil of straw on his head and sit with his feet lowered into a pool of water. One day...
253:
Filtering the drinking water, placing the water pot on his thigh, he stood waiting for the water drops to cease. At that time, the Elder gave this instruction (verse) to the novice:

“For one who is energetic, mindful, pure in deed, acting with consideration, restrained, living according to Dhamma, and heedful, fame increases.”

The novice applied that four-line verse to himself: “One like me should be energetic. One like me should be mindful... One like me should be heedful.” Having applied the verse to himself in this way, standing right there in that step, he cut the five lower fetters (saṃyojana) and, established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala), being joyful and satisfied, he uttered this inspired verse:

“I walked the cloister carrying a bundle of wet straw on my head; I have reached the third stage, the fruit of Non-returning; in this, I have no doubt.”

Thus, even while standing with weak supporting conditions (upannissaya), by striving and making an effort, he cut the five lower fetters and produced the three paths and fruits. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “If I were not, it would not be for me; it was not, it will not be for me—a monk reflecting thus could cut the lower fetters.”

In that passage, “No cassaṃ, no ca me siyā” means: If the collection of phenomena called ‘I’ were not to be, my requisites also would not be. Or, if past volitional formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra) had not occurred for me in the past, these five aggregates would not exist for me now. “Nābhavissa, na me bhavissati” means: Now I will strive so that the volitional formations (kammasankhāra) that produce the aggregates in the future will not occur; if that karma does not exist, future rebirth will not occur for me. “Evaṃ adhimuccamāno” means: A monk reflecting thus, even with weak supporting conditions, could cut the five lower fetters. “Evaṃ vutte” means: The Blessed One, reflecting on the emancipating nature of the Dispensation (Sāsana)...
254:
...when this inspired utterance was spoken. “Form will perish” means form will be destroyed. “Through the perishing of form” means seeing through insight (vipassanā) together with (the Path of Non-returning). Indeed, the four paths together with insight are called the seeing of the perishing of form and so on. This was said in reference to that (Path of Non-returning). “Venerable Sir, can a monk reflecting thus cut (the fetters)?” means: Venerable Sir, a monk reflecting thus indeed cuts the five lower fetters. The Blessed One considered, “Why would he not be able to cut them?”

Now, wishing to ask about the higher fruit of Arahatship, he said, “Venerable Sir, how...” and so on. In that passage, “anantara” refers to states that have no interval. There are two kinds: the near interval (āsannānantara) and the distant interval (dūrānantara). Insight is called the near interval of the Path, but the distant interval of the Fruit. In reference to that (the distant interval of the Fruit of Arahatship), he asked: “Venerable Sir, for one who knows and sees in what way does the fruit of Arahatship, known as the destruction of taints, occur immediately after insight?” “Atasitāya” means in a state where one should not be afraid. “Falls into terror” means reaching a state of fear. “That terror” refers to the weak insight (dubbala-vipassanā) that arises as “I shall not be, mine shall not be.” Because that insight cannot exhaust self-love (attasineha), terror arises in the uninstructed worldling. That worldling sees himself as if falling off a cliff, thinking, “Now I shall be annihilated, now nothing will exist.”

It is like a certain Brahmin. It is heard that beneath the Lohapāsāda, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga was reciting the Dhamma marked by the three characteristics. Then, to a Brahmin standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, formations appeared as empty (of self). He felt as if he were falling off a cliff, fled from there through the open door, and upon reaching home, placed his son on his chest and said, “Dear son, by reflecting on the doctrine of the Sakyan, my mind is ruined.” “There is no terror for that monk” means that strong insight (balava-vipassanā) arising in this way does not cause terror to an instructed noble disciple. For that noble disciple, there is no such reflection as “I shall be annihilated” or “I shall perish.” Rather, the reflection arises: “Only formations arise, only formations cease.” Therefore, there is no terror for the noble disciple. Even a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), though seeing formations as fearful, does not fall into terror. The commentary on the third sutta ends.

## 4. Upādānaparipavatta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, “catuparivaṭṭaṃ” means by way of the fourfold rotation (of the Four Noble Truths) in each aggregate. “Directly knew form” means he directly knew that form is the Truth of Suffering. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all terms.
255:
The meaning should be understood by way of the Four Truths. In the phrase "āhārasamudaya" (the origin of nutriment), physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) together with desire-and-lust, clinging, kamma, and ignorance is called "nutriment." "Paṭipanna" (those practicing) refers to those who are practicing from the purification of virtue up to the path of arahantship. "Gādhanti" means they gain a footing or stand firm. Having explained the plane of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi) with this sequence of words, the Blessed One now said, "Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave," and so forth, wishing to explain the plane of the non-trainee (asekkhabhūmi). "Suvimuttā" means those who are well-liberated by the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. "Kevalino" means those who have completed all tasks in their entirety. "Vaṭṭaṃ tesaṃ natthi paññāpanāya" means that there is no remaining round of existence (vaṭṭa) by which those non-trainees could be designated; that round of existence which exists for trainees for the purpose of designation no longer exists for these non-trainees. Alternatively, "vaṭṭa" means cause; thus, there is no longer a cause for designation. With this, the section on the plane of the non-trainee is concluded. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Sattaṭṭhāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "sattaṭṭhānakusala" (skilled in the seven bases) refers to one who is proficient in the seven instances (such as "he understands form," etc.). "Vusitavā" means one who has lived the holy life (ariya-vāsa). "Uttamapurisa" means the supreme man. The rest in this sutta should be understood according to the method already mentioned. Furthermore, this sutta should be known as both "Ussadanandiya" (Exalting and Delighting) and "Palobhanīya" (Alluring). Just as a king who has conquered in battle places the victorious warriors in high positions and honors them, so that other warriors, seeing their honors, will also strive to be brave; even so, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for an immeasurable time, conquered the Mara of defilements at the Great Bodhi Tree, attained omniscience, and while residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, delivered this sutta, exalting and praising the Arahants. For what reason? So that the remaining trainees (sekkhapuggala) would consider that the fruit of arahantship should be attained. Thus, this sutta is known as "Ussadanandiya" because it exalts and praises the Arahants, and "Palobhanīya" because it entices the trainees.

"Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled in the seven bases"—although the discourse was concluded with this sequence of words by way of the review of the paths and fruits, the Blessed One again said, "And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu an investigator in three ways?" This was said to show the constant abiding (satatavihāra) of the Arahant—that the object in which the Arahant constantly abides is not a being or a person, but merely elements and so forth—and to show the practice that is the way of arrival (āgamanīyapaṭipadā), expressed as "having performed work in these dhammas, this person has come." Therein, "dhātuso upaparikkhati" means he sees or observes by way of the nature of elements. In the remaining two terms, the method is the same. The fifth sutta is finished.
256:
## 6. Sammāsambuddha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "What is the distinction?" (ko adhippayāso) means "What is the special exertion (extraordinary effort)?" "Of the unarisen" (anuppannassa) means that Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One had brought this Noble Path into existence, but in the interval, no other teacher was able to bring it into existence; thus, the Blessed One is called the arouser of the unarisen path. Just as in a city, an ancient path exists in unused places, so in this context, it is called the unarisen path because it did not exist prior to the arising of the Buddha. "Of the unproduced" (asañjātassa) is a synonym for that same term "anuppannassa." "Of the unproclaimed" (anakkhātassa) means of the untold. Because he knows the path by his own knowledge, he is the "Knower of the Path" (maggannū). Because he made the path known and clear, like a gem in the palm of the hand, he is the "Cognizer of the Path" (maggavidū). Because he is skilled in what is the path and what is not the path, he is "Skilled in the Path" (maggakovido). "Path-followers" (maggānugā) are those who follow along the ancient path of the Buddha. "Attained afterwards" (pacchā samannāgatā) means "I went first (attained the path), and the disciples followed and attained it afterwards." The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "the group of five" (pañcavaggiye) refers to the five persons who were former attendants, such as the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. "He addressed" (āmantesi) means that starting from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, after they had gradually been established in the fruit of stream-entry, he addressed them on the fifth day of the fortnight, thinking, "Now I will teach the Dhamma to them for the destruction of the taints." "He said this" (etadavoca) means he spoke the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, which proceeds by way of "Form, bhikkhus, is non-self," and so forth. Therein, "non-self" (anattā) means non-self due to the four reasons mentioned previously. Why did he begin with "What do you think, bhikkhus?" Up to this point, only the characteristic of non-self had been taught, not the characteristics of impermanence and suffering; it should be understood that he began this to show those characteristics, and by combining them, to show all three characteristics. "Therefore" (tasmā) means because these five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. The detailed explanation of the phrases such as "whatever kind of form" has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the development of wisdom, under the description of the aggregates (Khandhaniddesa). The rest should be understood according to the method stated in all places. In this sutta, however, only the characteristic of non-self is taught. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Mahāli Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, the terms such as "exclusively suffering" (ekantadukkha) are according to the method already stated in the Dhātusaṃyutta. The eighth sutta is finished.
257:
## 9. Ādittasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, the Āditta Sutta, the term 'ādittaṃ' (burning) refers to being well-ablaze and flaming with the eleven fires, which begin with birth (jāti) and end with despair (upāyāsa). Thus, in both of these suttas, only the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) is taught. The ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Niruttipathasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the Niruttipatha Sutta, the term 'niruttipatha' (pathways of language) refers to the sounds or words that are the causes for explaining, deciding, and knowing various meanings. Alternatively, the grammatical analyses (viggaha) and etymologies (nibbacana) expressed with their reasons are also 'niruttipatha'. They are called 'niruttipatha' because they are the means of knowing meanings through the power of etymology. In the remaining two terms, 'adhivacanapatha' (pathways of designation) and 'paññattipatha' (pathways of concept), the same method of understanding should be applied. It should be understood that all three are merely synonyms (pariyāya-vevacana) of one another.

'Asaṅkiṇṇā' (unconfused) refers to things that are not abandoned. They are not discarded by saying, "What benefit is there in these pathways of language?" 'Asaṅkiṇṇapubbā' means they were not abandoned in the past. 'Na saṅkīyanti' means they are not being discarded now in the present by saying, "What benefit is there in these teachings?" 'Na saṅkīyissanti' means they will not be discarded in the future. 'Appaṭikuṭṭhā' refers to things that are not to be rejected. 'Atītaṃ' (past) refers to that which has transcended its own nature or has transcended dissolution (bhaṅga). 'Niruddhaṃ' (ceased) means having ceased and stilled right where it arose without moving to another place. 'Vipariṇataṃ' (changed) refers to that which has reached transformation or is destroyed. 'Ajātaṃ' (unborn) refers to that which has not yet arisen. 'Apātubhūtaṃ' (not manifested) refers to that which is not yet evident because it has not arisen.

'Ukkalā' refers to the inhabitants of the Ukkala region. 'Vassabhaññā' refers to the two individuals, Vassa and Bhañña. Both of them were holders of wrong views. In the passage starting with 'ahetukavādā', they are called 'ahetukavāda' (proponents of non-causality) because they hold the view that "there is no cause, no condition." They are called 'akiriyavāda' (proponents of non-action) because they hold that "for one who acts, no evil is done." They are called 'natthikavāda' (nihilists) because they hold views such as "there is nothing given (no fruit of giving)." In this context, it should be understood that each of these two individuals adopted all three of these views. This is like a monk who attains all four jhānas in succession. For one who repeatedly contemplates, attends to, delights in, and finds pleasure in the thought "there is no cause, no condition," it becomes as if they see the Path (but of wrongness). Such a person enters the fixed path of wrongness (micchatta-niyāma) and is called 'ekanta-kāḷaka' (utterly dark). Just as in the case of the view of non-causality, one also enters the fixed path of wrongness in these instances: "for one who acts, no evil is done" and "there is nothing given."

In the passage 'na garahitabbaṃ nappaṭikkositabbaṃ amaññiṃsu', one who says, "What is called past is not past; this is either future or present," is said to revile. One who shows faults therein and says, "What is the use of such reviling?" is also said to revile. In truth, those utterly dark holders of wrong views, Vassa and Bhañña, did not think that these pathways of language should be reviled or rejected. However, because they could not go against worldly convention, they spoke of the past as past, the future as future, and the present as present. Out of fear of the wise ones' blame, friction, and accusation...
258:
One who speaks (denying the past as past) is said to reject it. In truth, even those utterly dark holders of wrong views did not think that these pathways of language should be reviled or rejected. They spoke of the past as past, the future as future, and the present as present. 'Nindā-ghaṭṭana-byārosa-upārambha-bhaya' means out of fear of blame, fear of friction, fear of accusation, and fear of reproach from the wise. Thus, in this sutta, the designation (paññatti) of the aggregates (khandhas) belonging to the four planes (catubhūmika) is taught. The tenth sutta ends.

## Upayavagga, the Sixth.

## 7. Arahantavagga

## 1. Upādiyamānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Arahantavagga, 'upādiyamāno' refers to one who clings through the power of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi) (thinking "this is mine," etc.). 'Baddho mārassa' means being bound by the snare (of passion) of Māra. 'Mutto pāpimato' means being freed from the snare of the Evil One. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Maññamānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'maññamāno' refers to one who imagines through the imaginings (maññanā) of craving, conceit, and views. The second sutta ends.

## 3. Abhinandamānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'abhinandamāno' refers to one who greatly delights through the very delights of craving, conceit, and views. The third sutta ends.

## 4-5. Aniccasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
66-68. In the fourth sutta, 'chando' refers to the desire of craving (taṇhā-chanda). In the fifth and sixth suttas, the same method should be understood. The fourth and subsequent suttas end.

## 7. Anattaniyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'anattaniyaṃ' refers to the meaning of that which is not one's own, or that which is empty of being one's own requisite (parikkhāra). The seventh sutta ends.

## 4. Commentary on Arahanta Sutta
In the fourth sutta, 'Monks, as far as there are abodes of beings (sattāvāsa)' means, monks, as many as there are what are called abodes of beings. 'As far as there is the peak of existence (bhavagga)' means as much as there is what is called the peak of existence. 'These are the foremost, these are the best' means these are those who have become the foremost and those who have become the best. 'These Arahants' means those who are called Arahants. This sutta should also be understood as delighting by praising the virtues of the asekhas (adepts) who are endowed with many qualities, and as inducing the sekhas (trainees) and worldlings to strive by praising the virtues of the asekhas to inspire devotion, following the previous method.

'Thereafter, he said this' means he spoke the words beginning with 'The Arahants are truly happy' through verses that illustrate the meaning of that sutta and illustrate specific meanings. In those verses, 'happy' means they have reached happiness through the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of Fruition. 'Craving is not found in them' means the craving that produces the suffering of the lower realms is not found in them. Thus, they are truly happy due to the absence of the root of craving. 'The conceit "I am" is completely cut off' means the ninefold conceit (asmimāna) is completely cut off by the Path of Arahantship. 'The net of delusion is torn asunder' means the net of ignorance (avijjā) is torn apart by wisdom.

'The unmoved (anejaṃ)' means they have reached Arahantship, which is the abandonment of craving known as ejā. 'Unstained' means they are not stained by the coatings of craving and views. 'Become sublime (brahmabhūtā)' means they have become the best. 'Having fully understood' means having fully understood through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). 'Having the seven true dhammas as their domain' means faith...
260:
...faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, great learning, aroused energy, established mindfulness, and wisdom—these seven true dhammas (saddhamma) are their domain, thus they are 'sattasaddhammagocara'.

'Sattaratanasampannā' means being endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as jewels. 'Anuvicaranti' means that even worldly people wander about. However, in this Dispensation, it refers to the wandering without fear or hesitation (nirāsaṅkacāra) due to the absence of danger for the Arahants. Because they wander without such danger, it is said, "Those who have abandoned fear and dread." In that context, 'bhaya' refers to ordinary fear, while 'bherava' refers to intense fear. 'Dasahaṅgehi sampannā' means being endowed with the ten attributes of an asekha (Arahant). 'Mahānāgā' means they are called Great Nagas (noble beings like great elephants) due to four reasons. 'Samāhitā' means being firm and tranquil through access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā). "Craving is not found in them" means that even the enslaving craving, of which the Blessed One said, "Great King, the world is deficient, never satisfied, a slave to craving," no longer exists in those Arahants. By this, the state of being a master (bhujissa) who is liberated from the slavery of Arahants is shown.

'Asekha-knowledge' means the knowledge of the Fruition of Arahantship. 'Antimoyaṃ samussayo' means this physical body is the very last existence (attabhāva). In the phrase 'Yo sāro brahmacariyassa', 'sāra' (essence) refers to the Noble Fruition. 'Tasmim aparapaccayā' means in that Noble Fruition, they do not need to rely on others' faith but stand having personally realized and penetrated it. 'Vidhāsu na vikampanti' means they do not shake due to the three modes of conceit. 'Dantabhūmi' (the stage of the tamed) means Arahantship. 'Vijitāvino' means they stand having conquered the enemies of defilements such as lust.

In the words beginning with 'uddhaṃ', 'uddhaṃ' (above) refers to the tips of the hair, 'apācīnaṃ' (below) to the soles of the feet, and 'tiriyaṃ' (across) to the middle of the body. Alternatively, 'uddhaṃ' is the past, 'apācīnaṃ' is the future, and 'tiriyaṃ' is the present. Or, 'uddhaṃ' is the celestial realm, 'apācီnaṃ' is the lower realms, and 'tiriyaṃ' is the human realm. "Delight (nandī) is not found in them" means there is no craving in these places, or briefly, in the aggregates of the past, future, and present. Here, the absence of craving which is the root of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is shown. 'Buddha' means they are called Buddhas because they have realized the Four Noble Truths.

Here is the summary of the Lion's Roar (sīhanāda): "We are happy with the bliss of liberation, our craving that produces suffering is abandoned, the five aggregates are fully understood, the enslaving craving and the root-craving of the round are abandoned, we are peerless and sublime, we are Buddhas because of realizing the Four Noble Truths"—thus the Arahants, standing on the back of existence, roar the Lion's Roar, which is the fearless sound. The fourth sutta ends.
