## 5. Commentary on the Second Arahant Sutta

The fifth sutta is a discourse taught according to the inclination of those who can understand the Dhamma when it is delivered in a pure sequence without verses. The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Lion Sutta

In the sixth sutta, regarding "sīha" (lion), there are four types of lions: the grass lion (tiṇasīha), the black lion (kāḷasīha), the pale lion (paṇḍusīha), and the maned lion (kesarasīha). Among these four, the grass lion is like a pigeon-colored cow and eats grass. The black lion is like a black cow and also eats only grass. The pale lion is like a cow with the yellow color of a withered leaf and eats meat. The maned lion has a mouth, tail-tip, and four paws that are as red as if dyed with lac. From the head of that king of lions, there are three stripes that run down the middle of the back and circle to the right between the thighs, appearing as if drawn with a brush dipped in lac. On its neck, there is a mass of mane (kesara) as red as a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand. The remaining parts of its body are pure white, like the color of fine rice flour, powdered conch shell, or cotton. Among these four types of lions, the maned lion (kesarasīha) is intended in this sutta.

"Migarājā" means the king of beasts. "Āsayā" refers to coming out from its dwelling place, such as a golden cave, a silver cave, a ruby cave, a crystal cave, or a red arsenic (manosilā) cave. When that king of lions comes out, it does so for four reasons: either seeking light because it is oppressed by darkness, or to relieve itself of excrement and urine, or to seek food because it is oppressed by hunger, or to indulge in sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). In this sutta, however, coming out to seek food is intended.

"Vijambhati" means that on a surface of gold, silver, ruby, crystal, or red arsenic, it plants its two hind legs firmly, stretches its front legs forward, pulls the back part of its body and brings the front part forward, arches its back, lifts its neck, and snorts through its nostrils as if making a sound like thunder, shaking off the dust clinging to its body; this is the act of stretching and posturing. On the ground where it thus stretches, it runs to and fro like a young calf. As it runs, the body of that lion appears like a firebrand being whirled around in the darkness.
262:
"Anuviloketi" means: why does it look around? It is out of compassion for others. It is said that when that lion utters its roar, creatures such as elephants, gaurs, and buffaloes wandering in uneven places like precipices and pits might fall into those precipices or pits; it looks around out of compassion for those creatures. Does such a fierce lion that habitually eats the flesh of others really have compassion? Yes, it does. Indeed, that king of lions reflects, "What is the use of me killing many creatures?" and does not catch even small animals for the sake of its own food; thus it shows compassion. This has also been said: "May I not cause the destruction of small animals that have gone into difficult places" (A. Ni. 10.21).

"Sīhanādaṃ nadati" means that first, it utters a fearless roar three times. When it stands on the ground of its posturing and roars in this way, the sound creates a single resonance for three yojanas all around. Hearing that resonance, the groups of two-footed and four-footed creatures within the three yojanas are unable to remain in their usual places. "Gocarāya pakkamati" means it goes for the sake of food. How? Standing on the ground of its posturing, if it leaps to the right or to the left, it can cover a distance of one usabha. If it leaps upwards, it can leap four or eight usabhas. If it leaps straight on level ground, it can leap a distance of sixteen or twenty usabhas. If it leaps from a plateau or a mountain, it can leap a distance of sixty or eighty usabhas. If it sees a tree or a mountain in its path and avoids it, it swerves to the left or to the right by one usabha. Having uttered the lion's roar for the third time, it becomes manifest at a distance of three yojanas along with that sound. Having gone three yojanas, it turns back, stands, and listens to the echo of its own roar. In this way, it departs with great speed.

"Yebuyyena" means for the most part. Fear (bhaya), agitation (saṃvega), and terror (santāsa)—all three of these terms are names for mental alarm. Hearing the sound of the lion, many beings are afraid; a few are not afraid. Who are those who are not afraid? They are: an equal lion (samassīha), a noble elephant (hatthājānīya), a noble horse (assājānīya), a noble bull (usabhājānīya), a noble man (purisājānīya), and one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava/Arahant). Why do these not fear? An equal lion does not fear, reflecting, "I am equal in birth, lineage, clan, and courage." Noble elephants and others do not fear because of the strength of their self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). An Arahant does not fear because he has abandoned self-identity view.
263:
Bilāsaya refers to creatures that sleep or live in holes, such as snakes, mongooses, and monitor lizards. Dakāsaya refers to creatures that live in water, such as fish and turtles. Vanāsaya refers to creatures that live in the forest, such as elephants, horses, wild cattle, and deer. 'They enter' (pavisanti) means they enter while looking back at the path they came, thinking, 'He will come and catch me now.' 'Firm' (daḷhehi) means strong. 'With leather straps' (varattehi) means with leather ropes. In the terms such as 'possessing great power' (mahiddhiko), it should be understood as: the state of having great power (mahiddhikatā) by virtue of standing on the ground where it gambols and leaping straight for one usabha or with momentum for twenty usabhas; the state of having great authority (mahessakkhatā) by being the chief of other beasts; and the state of having great majesty (mahānubhāvatā) by virtue of creatures fleeing in terror upon hearing its thunderous roar within a radius of three yojanas.

In this way, the Blessed One taught about himself in various suttas in various ways. 'Monks, "Lion" is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One'—in this sutta, he first spoke of himself by making a comparison to a lion. 'Sunakkhatta, "the physician, the surgeon" is a designation for the Tathāgata'—in this sutta, he is compared to a physician. 'Monks, "Brahmin" is a designation for the Tathāgata'—in this sutta, he is compared to a Brahmin. 'Tissa, "the man skilled in the path" is a designation for the Tathāgata'—in this sutta, he is compared to a man who shows the way. 'Sela, I am a king'—in this sutta, he is compared to a king. However, in the sutta where he says, 'Lion is a designation for the Tathāgata,' he spoke of himself solely by making a comparison to a lion, saying thus:

The similarity in that teaching is as follows: Just as the time the lion dwells in a golden cave and so on, so should be understood the time the Tathāgata dwelt in the three palaces, enjoying prosperity similar to divine splendor when he reached maturity, having shaken the ten-thousandfold world system by his conception and his birth from his mother's womb in his final existence, after fulfilling the perfections for an immeasurable time since making his resolution at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. Just as the time the lion emerges from the golden cave and so on, so the Tathāgata, in his twenty-ninth year, emerged through the open gate mounted on the horse Kanthaka with his companion Channa, crossed three kingdoms, and on the banks of the river Anomā, [received] the [robes] offered by the Brahma...
264:
...having donned the saffron robes and ordained, on the seventh day he went to the city of Rājagaha for alms, and after finishing his meal at the cave of Mount Paṇḍava, he traveled to the Magadha kingdom first to attain Supreme Enlightenment and until the time he received the promise from the King [Bimbisāra]. (This is to be understood as the time similar to the lion's awakening/stretching.)

Just like the time of the lion's gamboling, it should be understood as the period from when the Blessed One, having given his promise, approached Āḷāra Kālāma, until the time he consumed the forty-nine morsels of milk-rice offered by Sujātā. Just like the lion's shaking of its mane, it should be understood as the time when, in the evening, he accepted the eight handfuls of grass offered by the grass-cutter Sotthiya, and being praised and honored with scents and so on by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times, ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa, spread the grass mat on a spot fourteen cubits high, and resolved upon the fourfold effort. At that very moment, he dispelled the army of Māra, purified the three knowledges during the three watches of the night, and while churning the great ocean of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order with the churning-stick of the Knowledge of Pairs (Yamaka-ñāṇa), he penetrated the Knowledge of Omniscience, at which the ten-thousandfold world system shook through its power.

Just like the lion's looking in the four directions, it should be understood as the time when, after penetrating the Knowledge of Omniscience, he dwelt at the Bodhimaṇḍa for seven weeks, and after consuming the meal of honey-balls, he accepted the request of the Great Brahma Sahampati to teach the Dhamma at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree. While staying there, on the dawn of the eleventh day, he reflected, 'Tomorrow will be the full moon of Āsāḷha; to whom should I first teach the Dhamma?' Knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he looked for the group of five monks to teach them the Dhamma. Just like the time the lion travels three yojanas for prey, it should be understood as the time when, taking his bowl and robes, he reflected, 'I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma for the group of five monks,' and after his meal, he rose from the Ajapāla Banyan tree and traveled the eighteen-yojana journey.

Just like the time of the lion's roar, it should be understood as the time when the Tathāgata, having traveled the eighteen-yojana journey and convinced the group of five monks, sat on the unshakable throne, surrounded by the host of deities assembled from the ten thousand world-systems, and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the manner beginning with: 'Monks, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth.' While this discourse was being taught, the sound of the Dhamma of the Tathāgata-Lion spread from the Avīci hell below to the highest heaven (Bhavagga) above.
265: (The Buddha) pervades the ten thousand world systems. Just as small creatures are terrified by the roar of a lion, one should understand the time when the long-lived deities experience the dread of knowledge (ñāṇasantāsa) while the Tathāgata, having revealed the three characteristics and analyzed the Four Noble Truths through sixteen modes and sixty thousand methods, preaches the Dhamma. "Yadā" means at which time. "Tathāgato" means the Blessed One is called Tathāgata for eight reasons. They are: Tathāgata because He has come in the same way as previous Buddhas (tathā āgato); Tathāgata because He has gone in the same way as previous Buddhas (tathā gato); Tathāgata because He has arrived at the true characteristics (tatha-lakkhaṇaṃ āgato); Tathāgata because He has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they really are (tatha-dhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); Tathāgata because He sees things as they really are (tatha-dassitāya); Tathāgata because He speaks things as they really are (tatha-vāditāya); Tathāgata because He acts as He speaks (tatha-kāritāya); and Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming everything (abhibhavanaṭṭhena). The details of these eight reasons have already been stated in the commentaries on the Brahmajāla Sutta and the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. "Loke" refers to the world of beings. "Uppajjati" means from the time of the initial aspiration until the seat of enlightenment or the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, it is called "arising"; however, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, it is called "having arisen." The attributes such as "Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho" have been explained in detail in the Buddhānussati-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga. "Iti rūpaṃ" means this form is only this much; there is no form beyond this. By this much, all the four great elements and the derived form (upādā-rūpa) dependent on the four great elements are shown in terms of their nature, their own function, their limit, and their delimitation. "Iti rūpassa samudayo" means this is the cause of the arising of form. By this much, everything such as "with the arising of nutriment, form arises" is shown. "Iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo" means this is the cessation of form. By this much, everything such as "with the cessation of nutriment, form ceases" is shown. The same method applies to "Iti vedanā" and so on. "Vaṇṇavanto" means possessing beauty of body. "Dhamma-desanaṃ sutvā" means having heard this Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, which is adorned with fifty characteristics regarding the five aggregates. In the word "yebhuyyena" (mostly), who are excluded here? The noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) deities are excluded. For those noble ones, because their taints are destroyed, the fear of mental agitation does not arise. For one who is terrified, by striving through appropriate means...
266:
For the individuals whose taints are destroyed (akhīṇāsava) and who have reached the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), spiritual urgency through knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvega) does not arise because they have already attained what was to be attained. However, for other deities who are not akhīṇāsava, when they reflect on impermanence, thinking, 'O monks, these five aggregates are terrifying,' mental terror (cittutrāsa) arises, and during the time of powerful insight, fear through knowledge (ñāṇabhaya) together with moral dread (ottappa) arises. This term 'fear' (bhaya) is merely a conventional expression used in reference to the Dhamma which is devoid of a person. 'Included in the identity' (sakkāyapariyāpanna) means being included within the five aggregates. Thus, when the Blessed One shows the faults of the round of rebirths to those long-lived deities and Brahmas and teaches the Dhamma by applying the three characteristics, the terror known as fear through knowledge (ñāṇabhaya) descends upon them.

Abhiññāya means having known. The Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) refers to both the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedhañāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa). The knowledge of penetration is that knowledge by which, while seated on the throne of enlightenment, He penetrated the Four Noble Truths through sixteen modes and sixty thousand methods. The knowledge of teaching is that knowledge by which He set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, which has three rounds and twelve modes. Both of these are knowledges born in the heart of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha). Among these two, the knowledge of teaching should be taken here. The Blessed One set that knowledge of teaching in motion until the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) arose for the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña along with eighteen crores of Brahmas. It should be understood that when that fruit of stream-entry arose, the Wheel of Dhamma was said to be set in motion (taught). Appaṭipuggala means a person without an equal. Yasassino means those endowed with a retinue. Tādino means one who remains the same in the face of worldly conditions such as gain and loss. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Khajjanīyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, the phrase 'past lives' (pubbenivāsa) is not spoken with reference to recollection by means of direct knowledge (abhiññā), but with reference to recluses and brahmins who recollect their former dwellings by means of insight (vipassanā). Therefore, He said: 'All those [recluses and brahmins] recollect these five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them.' For one who recollects by means of direct knowledge, the aggregates, the aggregates of clinging, things connected with the aggregates, and even concepts can be the object. In saying 'he recollects only form,' such a person who recollects does not recollect any other being or person, but recollects only the aggregate of form that had ceased in the past. The same method applies to feeling and so on. The section on emptiness (suññatāpabba) is finished.

Now, to show the characteristic of emptiness, He said: 'Monks, what do you call form?' and so forth. For example, a man searching for a lost ox, while wandering among a herd of cattle, might see a red or black bull, but he cannot decide 'this is my ox' merely by seeing that much color.
267:
One cannot make a decision. Why? Because there are other cows of similar appearance. But seeing a mark such as a spear or a trident on a part of its body, the decision arises: "This cow is my property." Similarly, even if emptiness (suññatā) is taught, as long as the characteristic of emptiness is not taught, it is as if it has not been taught. Only when the characteristic is taught is it said to be taught. Emptiness is like the cow; the characteristic of emptiness is like the mark of the spear or trident on the cow. Just as a cow is not well-recognized if its mark is not recognized, but is recognized when the mark is recognized, so too, if the characteristic of emptiness is not taught, emptiness remains untaught; only when that characteristic is taught is emptiness said to be taught. Therefore, to show the characteristic of emptiness, the Buddha said: "Monks, what do you call form (rūpa)?" and so on.

In that text, "kañca" is a question about the cause. For what reason do they call it form? For what reason is this group [of phenomena] called form? This is the meaning. In the sentence "ruppatīti kho," the word "iti" indicates the reason. It means it is called form because it is "deformed" (ruppati). "Ruppati" means it is affected, struck, oppressed, or broken. In the passages such as "it is deformed by cold," the deformation by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. Between every three world-systems (cakkavāḷas), there is one Lokantarika hell, measuring eighty thousand yojanas. Below it, there is no earth; above it, there is no light from the moon, sun, lamps, or gems; it is perpetual darkness. The beings born there have bodies measuring three gāvutas. Like bats, they cling to the foot of the [Cakkavāḷa] mountains with long, wide nails, hanging upside down. When, while crawling, they come within reach of one another's hands, they think, "We have found food!" and in their effort to seize [the other], they lose their grip and fall into the water that supports the world. Even when the cold wind blows, they are severed from their hold like madhuka fruits and fall into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve with a "pata-pata" sound in that extremely cold water, like a lump of flour falling into hot oil. Thus, deformation by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. It is also evident in very cold regions where snow falls, such as the Mahimsaka kingdom. There, beings' bodies are broken by the cold, and they even reach the end of their lives.

Deformation by heat is evident in the Great Avīci Hell. Deformation by hunger is evident in the realm of Petas and during times of famine. Deformation by thirst is evident among the Kālakañjika Asuras and others. How? It is said that a Kālakañjika Asura, unable to endure his thirst, went down to the great Ganges River, which is a hundred yojanas wide. Wherever that Peta reached, the water disappeared and steam arose. It felt as if a hot stone slab or a hot potsherd had been placed inside his belly. While wandering here and there searching for the sound of water in that river, the night turned into dawn. Then, about thirty monks coming for alms early in the morning saw that Peta and asked, "Friend, who are you?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I am a Peta." When asked, "What are you searching for?" he replied, "I am searching for drinking water." They said, "Do you not see this Ganges River full of water?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, it does not appear so to me." They said, "If so, lie down on the sandbank of the Ganges; we will pour water into your mouth." Thus, that Peta lay down on the sandbank.
268:
Unable to endure thirst, he descended into the great Gaṅgā river, which is a hundred yojanas wide. However, wherever that Peta went, the water disappeared, and smoke and flames arose. It was as if there were hot stone slabs or a hot potsherd in his belly. Hearing the sound of water in that river, he wandered here and there, and while searching, the night turned into dawn. Then, thirty monks who were going for alms early in the morning saw that Peta and asked, "Good man, who are you?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I am a Peta." When asked, "What are you searching for?", he replied, "Venerable sirs, I am searching for drinking water." They said, "This Gaṅgā river is full of water; do you not see it?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, it is not apparent to me (I cannot see it)." They said, "If so, lie down on the sandy bank of the Gaṅgā; we will pour water into your mouth." So the Peta lay on his back on the sand. The monks took water with their thirty alms-bowls and poured it into the Peta's mouth. While they were repeatedly carrying and pouring water, the time for alms-round drew near. Then they asked, "O good man, it is time for our alms-round; did you receive even a little taste of water?" The Peta swore and said, "Venerable sirs, if even as much as half a handful of the water poured from the thirty bowls of the thirty noble ones reached my throat, may I never be released from this state of a Peta." Thus, in the Peta realm, deformation (ruppana) due to thirst is very evident.

Deformation due to gadflies, mosquitoes, and so on is evident in places where they are abundant. Here, 'ḍaṃsa' refers to a pale-colored gadfly. 'Makasa' is simply a mosquito. 'Vāta' (wind) should be understood as wind-related diseases caused by internal gases in the stomach, back, etc. When wind diseases arise in the body, they can damage the hands, feet, back, etc., and cause blindness, hunching, or the need to move with the aid of a stool. 'Ātapa' refers to the heat of the sun. Deformation due to that sun-heat is evident in waterless, difficult desert journeys. It is heard that a woman was left behind by a caravan in the desert at night. When the sun rose during the day, the sand became so hot that she could not set foot on it, so she took the basket from her head and stepped on it. Gradually, the basket also became hot from the sun's heat, and unable to stand, she spread a cloth over it and stepped on that. When that cloth also became hot, she laid down her young child, whom she was carrying at her waist, face down and stepped on the crying child. In that very place, both mother and child died due to the heat of the sun.

'Sarisapa' refers to any long-bodied creeping creature. Deformation due to contact and bites from these creatures should be understood through the power of poisonous cobra bites and so on. Thus, among the two characteristics—the general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) and the individual characteristic (paccatta-lakkhaṇa)—the Blessed One first showed the individual characteristic of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). This nature of deformation (ruppana) is the specific characteristic of the aggregate of form alone; it is not a characteristic of feeling and so on. Therefore, it is called the individual characteristic. The characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta), however, are also characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, those characteristics are called general characteristics. In the Pali texts beginning with "And what, bhikkhus, do you call form?", it should be understood according to the characteristic of the aggregate of form mentioned earlier. This statement is different from the previous one and is an explanation to make it clear. "He feels pleasure" means experiencing a pleasant object. In the two sentences "He feels pain" and "He feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure", it should be understood in the same way. If asked why that object is called pleasant, painful, or neither-pain-nor-pleasant, it is because it assists pleasant feeling and so on through the power of condition (paccaya-satti). This meaning is obtained according to the method found in the Mahāli Sutta.
269:
(That deformation) is called the individual characteristic (paccatta-lakkhaṇa). The characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta) also occur in feeling and so on; therefore, those characteristics are called general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa).

"And what, bhikkhus, do you call feeling?" In the Pali texts beginning with this, the parts similar to the aggregate of form mentioned earlier should be understood in the same way as already stated. The explanation for the part that is not similar to the previous statement is as follows: "He also feels pleasure" means he feels or experiences a pleasant object. In the next two terms as well, the method is the same. Why is that object called pleasant, painful, or neither-pain-nor-pleasant? It is because it assists as a condition for pleasant feeling and so on. This meaning is just as it appears in this Mahāli Sutta: "Mahāli, because form is pleasant, follows pleasure, and descends into pleasure." In this term "feels", it is feeling alone that feels; no other being or person feels. Since feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, feeling alone feels depending on the base and the object. Thus, here, the Blessed One showed only the individual characteristic of feeling by analyzing it.

"He also perceives blue" means that by performing preliminary work (parikamma) on a blue flower or cloth, he perceives it while reaching access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā). This perception (saññā) can be preliminary perception, access perception, or absorption perception; the perception that arises as "blue, blue" is also valid. In the case of yellow and so on, the method is the same. Here too, the Blessed One showed only the individual characteristic of perception, which has the characteristic of perceiving, by analyzing it.

"They condition the conditioned for the sake of form-state" means just as one cooks gruel to be gruel or a cake to be a cake, so form, which has received the name "conditioned" (saṅkhata) because it is made by the meeting of conditions, is conditioned for the sake of form-state so that it becomes what is called conditioned form; it means one strives, accumulates, and produces it for that state, for the state of being form. In the case of feeling and so on, the method is the same. The summary here is: it specifically conditions and produces the form that arises together with itself, as well as the associated states such as feeling and so on. Here too, the Blessed One showed only the individual characteristic of mental formations (saṅkhāra), which has the characteristic of volition (cetayita), by analyzing it.

"He also cognizes the sour taste" means he cognizes sour objects such as mango, wood-apple, and citron as "sour". In all terms, the method is the same. Furthermore, here, "bitter taste" refers to various bitter objects such as neem and bitter gourd. "Pungent taste" refers to various pungent objects such as long pepper and black pepper. Sweet taste means...
270:
It refers to various sweet-tasting substances such as ghee, molasses, and so forth. 'Khārikaṃ' refers to various salty or briny substances such as eggplant, kone-karu, spinach, cane shoots, and so forth. 'Akhārikaṃ' refers to any tasteless fruit or mixed leaves such as tasteless kapyin leaves. 'Loṇikaṃ' refers to various salty-tasting substances such as overly salty gruel, salty fish, salty rice, and so forth. 'Aloṇikaṃ' refers to various low-salt or unsalted substances such as unsalted gruel, unsalted fish, unsalted rice, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Therefore, it is called consciousness (viññāṇa)": it is because it knows the various tastes such as the aforementioned sourness, etc., through their mutually distinct nature as sourness and so forth. Because it knows through such mutually distinct natures, it is called consciousness. Thus, in this description of consciousness, the Blessed One has analyzed and shown only the individual characteristic (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) of consciousness, which has the characteristic of cognizing through mutually distinct modes.

Because perception (saññā) becomes manifest through the grasping of the modes and shapes of an object, such as its color, length, and so forth, or its circular or square form, it is analyzed in the eye-door. Because consciousness (viññāṇa) becomes manifest through the grasping of the specific individual nature of various objects even without grasping their modes and shapes, it is analyzed in the tongue-door. To understand the nature of these three—perception, consciousness, and wisdom (paññā)—without confusion, the distinction between the terms "sañjānāti" (perceives), "vijānāti" (cognizes), and "pajānāti" (understands) should be understood. In these terms, the distinction lies only in the prefixes "saṃ", "vi", and "pa", while the word "jānāti" (knows) is common to all. Even in that word "jānāti", the distinction should be understood by the sense of knowing.

Indeed, perception is only able to perceive the object by way of its color, such as blue, etc.; it is not able to reach the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Consciousness knows the object by way of its color, such as blue, etc., and also reaches the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, etc.; however, it is not able to further advance insight to reach the manifestation of the Path (magga). Wisdom knows the object by way of its color, such as blue, etc., reaches the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, etc., and is also able to further advance insight to reach the manifestation of the Path.

To illustrate this meaning with an analogy: suppose a heap of coins (kahāpaṇa) is placed on a money-changer's counter, and three people—an inexperienced child, a villager, and an expert money-changer—stand looking at it. The inexperienced child knows only the varied colors and the square or circular shapes of the coins; he does not know, "This is an object considered a treasure suitable for human use and consumption." The villager knows both the varied appearance and that it is a treasure suitable for human use; however, he does not distinguish, "This coin is a counterfeit, this one is genuine, this one is rough, or this one is smooth." The expert money-changer, however, knows the varied appearance, its status as a treasure, and whether it is counterfeit or genuine. While knowing this...
271:
Furthermore, (the expert money-changer), by seeing the appearance, hearing the sound, smelling the scent, tasting the flavor, and weighing it in his hand, knows, "It was made in such-and-such a village." He also knows, "It was made in such-and-such a market town, such-and-such a city, under the shadow of such-and-such a mountain, or on the bank of such-and-such a river." He even knows, "It was made by such-and-such a master."

In the same way, perception (saññā) knows only the object by way of blue, etc., like the inexperienced child's seeing of the coins. Consciousness (viññāṇa) knows the object by way of blue, etc., and also reaches the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, etc., like the villager's seeing of the coins. Wisdom (paññā) knows the object by way of blue, etc., reaches the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, etc., and further advances insight to reach the manifestation of the Path, like the expert money-changer's seeing of the coins.

That distinction (between consciousness and wisdom) is difficult to penetrate. Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said: 
"Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task." 
"Venerable Nāgasena, what difficult task has the Blessed One performed?" 
"Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task in declaring the distinction of these immaterial mental states of mind and mental factors (citta-cetasika) that arise in a single object, saying: 'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is mind.'"

Just as if five kinds of oil—sesame oil, mustard oil, mahua oil, castor oil, and animal fat—were poured into a single pot and stirred with a whisk all day, it would be difficult to extract each one separately, saying, "This is sesame oil, this is mustard oil"; this (distinguishing of mental states) is even more difficult than that. However, the Blessed One, being the Lord of Dhamma and the King of Dhamma, because of His well-penetrated Omniscient Knowledge, made the distinction of these immaterial states that arise in a single object. This meaning should also be understood by the analogy of extracting water separately where the five great rivers enter the ocean, saying, "This is the water of the Gaṅgā, this is the water of the Yamunā."

Thus, having taught the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) through these two groups—emptiness (suññata) by the first group and the characteristic of emptiness by the second group—He now says "Tatra bhikkhave," etc., to show the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa). In that passage, "khajjāmi" (I am being eaten) does not mean that the material form (rūpa) tears and eats flesh like a dog. Rather, it should be understood as when a person wearing dirty clothes says, "The clothes are eating me," referring to the oppression caused by that reason.
272:
Just as it is said in the world, "The clothes are eating me," in the same way, this form should be understood as "eating" or "consuming" by causing oppression and affliction. "Paṭipanno hoti" means one practices from virtue (sīla) up to the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Among these practitioners, a noble person with strong wisdom, sharp wisdom, and superior wisdom, while striving in the meditation ground, might be pierced by a stump or a thorn, struck by a weapon, or seized and bitten by a tiger or such. Yet, disregarding that painful feeling, he constantly contemplates the original meditation subject (mūla-kammaṭṭhāna) and attains the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). Such a noble person is called one who practices for the sake of revulsion, dispassion, and cessation regarding feeling. This is like Elder Pītamalla, Elder Kuṭumbiyaputta Mahātissa, the monk lying in the tiger's mouth among the thirty monks in the Vattani forest, and the Elder pierced by a thorn.

It is said that while twelve monks were practicing meditation in the forest after striking the gong, one monk, just as the sun was setting, struck the gong, descended to the walkway, and while walking, stepped on a thorn hidden by grass. The thorn went right through to the top of his foot. A feeling arose as if he were being pierced by a hot iron spit. That Elder thought, "Should I pull out this thorn, or should I pull out the permanent thorn (of defilements)?" Then he reflected, "There is no danger in hell or elsewhere because of being pierced by this external thorn; I will only pull out the five thorns (of defilements) which are permanent and difficult to abandon." Disregarding that feeling, he walked on the walkway all night, and when dawn broke, he gave a signal to another monk. That monk came and asked, "What is it, Bhante?" "Friend, I have been pierced by a thorn." "At what time, Bhante?" "Just in the evening, friend." "Why did you not call us? We would have pulled out the thorn and poured oil on it." "Friend, I was striving without regard for my life to pull out only the five thorns (of defilements) which are permanent and difficult to abandon." "Bhante, were you able to pull them out?" "Friend, I have pulled them out with the mind (through the path-knowledge)." The remaining stories are detailed in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta description in the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāya Commentaries.

Why was the phrase "What do you think, monks?" started? In this section, only the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) has been taught, and the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) has not yet been taught. This section was started to show that characteristic of impermanence, and also to show the three characteristics combined. "Apacināti no ācināti" means he destroys the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and does not accumulate it. "Pajahati na upādiyati" means he abandons that very cycle and does not grasp it. "Vikirati na ussinati" means he scatters it and does not collect it. "Vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti" means that which is called the three cycles...
273:
...does not take. "Visineti na ussineti" means he scatters and does not collect or accumulate. "Vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti" means he extinguishes and does not kindle, or he cools and does not let burn. Why was the phrase "Seeing thus, monks" started? It was started to show the Great Arahant (khīṇāsava) who stands having destroyed the cycle of existence. Or, with this much of the Pali, insight (vipassanā) has been taught; now this is started to show the four paths together with insight. Or, with this much of the Pali, the first path has been taught; now this is started to show the three higher paths together with insight. Or, with this much of the Pali, the three paths have been taught; now this is started to show the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) together with insight. "Sapajāpatikā" means together with the king of gods, Pajāpati. "Ārakāva namassanti" means they pay homage even from a distance; they pay homage to the Arahant who stands even far away, just as they paid homage to the Venerable Elder Nīta. 

It is heard that the Elder, having left a family of flower-scavengers and ordained, attained the fruit of Arahantship even at the tip of the razor (during his tonsure) and thought: "I have ordained this very day, and this very day my task of monkhood has reached its completion; I shall fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (Mahā-ariyavaṃsa), adorned with contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation." That Elder entered Sāvatthī for the sake of refuse-heap rags (paṃsukūla) and wandered searching for worn-out cloth. Then a Mahābrahmā, having emerged from an attainment and looking at the path of humans, saw the Elder and stood paying homage with joined palms, thinking, "He ordained this very day, attained Arahantship at the tip of the razor this very day, and is searching for worn-out cloth to fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage." Another Mahābrahmā saw him paying homage and asked, "To whom are you paying homage?" "I am paying homage to Elder Nīta." "For what reason?" "Because he ordained this very day, attained Arahantship at the tip of the razor this very day, and is searching for worn-out cloth to fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage." That questioning Brahma also stood paying homage to the Elder. Furthermore, seven hundred other Mahābrahmās stood paying homage. Therefore, it is said:

"Those seven hundred noble deities,
Having come out from the Brahma mansions,
With confident minds, pay homage to Nīta,
(Saying) 'The Arahant is taking the refuse-heap rags.'"
274:
Those seven hundred noble deities, having come out from the Brahma mansions, with confident hearts, pay homage to the Elder Nīta: 'The Arahant seeks a rag-robe,' 'The Arahant washes the rag-robe,' 'The Arahant dyes the rag-robe,' 'The Arahant wears the rag-robe.'

Thus the Blessed One, in this Sutta, having turned the discourse through the three rounds of existence, led it to the peak of Arahantship. At the end of the discourse, five hundred monks were established in Arahantship. The seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Piṇḍolyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth Sutta, 'kismiñcideva pakaraṇe' means for some reason. 'Paṇāmetvā' means having dismissed (having removed from his presence). For what reason did the Blessed One dismiss those monks? Once, the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the end of the retreat. Surrounded by a large Saṅgha of monks, he left Sāvatthī and wandered through the countryside, arriving at Kapilavatthu and entering the Nigrodhārāma monastery. The Sakyan kings, hearing that 'the Teacher has arrived,' brought suitable items such as oil, honey, molasses, and drinks on hundreds of carrying-poles after their meal. They went to the monastery, offered them to the Saṅgha, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place after exchanging greetings. The Teacher sat there, preaching a sweet Dhamma talk to those kings.

At that moment, some monks were cleaning the lodgings, some were spreading out couches and stools, and novices were clearing away grass. There were monks present at the place where the gift items were being distributed, and some who had not yet arrived. Those who were present, while taking shares for those who had not arrived, made a great noise, shouting, 'Give to us! Give to our teacher! Give to our preceptor!' The Teacher, hearing that noise, asked the Venerable Ānanda, 'Ānanda, what is that loud noise, that great noise, like that of fishermen at a haul of fish?' The Elder Ānanda reported the matter. Hearing this, the Teacher said, 'Ānanda, the monks are making a great noise for the sake of material things (āmisa).' 'Yes, Bhante,' he replied. 'Ānanda, this is not fitting, it is not proper.'
275:
'I did not fulfill the perfections for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of robes and such. Nor did these monks go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes and such. Having gone forth for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship, they are making what is not beneficial appear as beneficial, and what is essence-less appear as having essence. Go, Ānanda, dismiss those monks.'

'Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ' means the morning of the second day. 'Beluvalaṭṭhikāya mūle' means at the foot of a young bael tree. 'Pabāḷho' means dismissed or cast out. There is also a variant reading 'pavāḷho,' which has the same meaning as 'pavāhita' (dismissed). Both terms indicate the state of being removed. 'Siyā aññathattaṃ' means there might be a change in devotion or a change in one's state. How? Thinking, 'The Fully Enlightened One dismissed us for a minor reason,' and thus having their devotion decrease is called 'change in devotion' (pasāda-aññathatta). Going to a monastery of non-Buddhists while still in the form of a monk is called 'change in state' (bhāva-aññathatta). Regarding 'siyā vipariṇāmo' in this context: Thinking, 'We went forth thinking we could grasp the Teacher's intention, but since we cannot, what is the use of our monkhood?' and then abandoning the training and returning to the low life of a layman is known as 'transformation' (vipariṇāma).

'Vacchassa' refers to a suckling calf. 'Aññathattaṃ' means a change through withering. Indeed, a suckling calf, not seeing its mother and not getting milk, withers and trembles. 'Vipariṇāmo' means death. That suckling calf, not getting milk and thirsting for it, dries up, falls, and dies.

'Bījānaṃ taruṇānaṃ' refers to newly sprouted seeds that should be supported by water. 'Aññathattaṃ' is simply withering. Those seeds wither when they do not get water. 'Vipariṇāmo' means destruction. Those seeds, not getting water, dry up and perish, becoming nothing but straw. 'Anuggahito' means supported by both material support (āmisa-anuggaha) and Dhamma support (dhamma-anuggaha). 'Anuggaṇheyyaṃ' means 'I should support' with these two kinds of support. Indeed, novices and young monks who have recently gone forth, if they lack requisites like robes or are ill, and are not supported with material things by the Teacher or their teachers and preceptors, become weary and cannot perform recitation or mental reflection. If they are not supported by Dhamma support—through instruction, advice, and admonition—they decline and cannot abandon unwholesome states and develop wholesome ones. However, if they are supported by these two kinds of support, they do not become weary in body and can engage in recitation and mental reflection according to the instructions...'
276: Even if those practicing monks do not receive such support later on, they are able to remain firm in the Dispensation through the strength of the support they received previously. Therefore, this thought arose to the Blessed One. "Appeared before the Blessed One" means: Having known the mind of the Teacher, thinking, "The Blessed One dismissed these monks, but now he wishes to favor them and is thinking thus; I shall exert effort in this matter," he became manifest before him. Regarding the words "Sante'ttha bhikkhū" (There are monks here), just as a clever cook prepares the sour flavors and such that the King likes to be even more delicious and offers them the next day, so too, through his own cleverness, the Great Brahmā refined the very simile brought forth by the Blessed One with words such as "Evaṃ etaṃ Bhagavā" (So it is, Blessed One) and requested the Blessed One for the sake of favoring the Saṅgha of monks. In that context, "Abhinandatu" means "May the Saṅgha of monks come to my presence," thus may he rejoice in their coming. "Abhivadatu" means may he address them by giving exhortation and instruction to those who have arrived. "Paṭisallānā" means being alone. "Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi" means he performed a feat of psychic power. "Ekadvīhikāyā" means being one by one or two by two. "Sārajjamānarūpā" means having a nature of being bashful or fearful. Why did the Blessed One perform such a feat of psychic power for them to approach in that manner? It was out of a desire for their welfare. For if those monks had come in groups, they might have mocked him, saying, "The Blessed One dismissed the Saṅgha of monks and entered the forest, but was unable to stay there even for a single day and has returned in haste." If that happened, they would not have respect for the Buddha and would not be able to receive the Dhamma teaching. However, thinking that if they come one by one or two by two, being fearful and bashful, respect for the Buddha will be established and they will be able to receive the Dhamma teaching, he performed such a feat of psychic power out of a desire for their welfare. "Nisīdiṃsu" (They sat down): When they arrived in that bashful manner, one monk, thinking, "The Teacher is looking only at me; I think he wants to rebuke only me," came slowly, paid homage, and sat down. Then another, then another, and so the five hundred monks sat down. Seeing the Saṅgha of monks thus seated, as still as the great ocean situated between the Sīdantara mountains or like a lamp in a windless place, the Teacher thought: "I dismissed these monks for a certain reason, but now only the teaching on morsels of alms-food is suitable; I shall preach that Dhamma."
277: "What kind of Dhamma teaching is suitable for these monks?" (The Blessed One thought). Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "These monks were dismissed because of food; only the Dhamma teaching concerning morsels of alms-food is suitable for them. Having shown that teaching, I shall preach the Tiparivaṭṭa (three-round) teaching at the end. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the monks will reach Arahantship." Then, while preaching that Dhamma teaching to them, he said, "Monks, this way of life is the lowest," and so on. In that text, "Anta" means the last or the vile. "Yadidaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ" refers to the livelihood of one who makes a living by seeking alms in this way. The meaning of this term is: because one wanders for the sake of alms (piṇḍāya ulati), one is called "piṇḍola"; the state or action of a piṇḍola is "piṇḍolyaṃ," meaning a livelihood accomplished by seeking alms. "Abhisāpa" means a curse or abuse. Angry people curse their enemies, saying, "May you wander seeking alms, wearing robes and carrying a bowl-shard." Or else they abuse them, saying, "What is there that you should not do, you who, though endowed with such strength and energy, have abandoned shame and fear and wander like a destitute person, a piṇḍola with a bowl in hand?" "Tañca kho etaṃ" means that although this piṇḍolya (alms-gathering) is like such a curse, sons of good family in my Dispensation—whether by birth or by conduct—being motivated by a purpose or a specific reason, approach (ordain) based on that reason. In the terms "Rājābhinītā" and so on: those who, having consumed the king's property, were imprisoned by the king and fled from prison to ordain are called "Rājābhinītā" (driven by the king). They are so called because they were driven to the king's bonds. Those who were captured by thieves in the forest, and while some were being killed, some pleaded, "Sirs, if you release us, we will not return home but will ordain; in that monkhood, we will perform meritorious deeds such as Buddha-pūjā and share the merit with you," and were thus released by the thieves to ordain, are called "Corābhinītā" (driven by thieves). They are so called because they were driven to the state of being killed by thieves. Those who took debts and, being unable to repay them, fled and ordained are called "Iṇaṭṭhā," meaning those oppressed by debt (there is also a reading "Iṇaṭṭhā" meaning those standing in debt). Those who ordain being overwhelmed and harassed by any one of the fears—fear of the king, fear of thieves, fear of famine, or fear of disease—are called "Bhayaṭṭhā," meaning those oppressed by fear (there is also a reading "Bhayaṭṭhā" meaning those standing in fear). "Ājīvakasapakato" means one who ordains because he is oppressed by the matter of livelihood and is unable to support his wife and children. "Otiṇṇā" means having objects of sorrow pierced into the heart. The words "Socati" and so on are as follows...
278:
It means they stand in fear. Ājīvikāpakata means being oppressed and overwhelmed by the means of livelihood, such that they are unable to support their wives and children. Otiṇṇa means that objects of grief have pierced into the heart.

The phrase "He is also one of much covetousness" was spoken to show that although that son of a good family went forth with the thought, "I will make an end of suffering," and so forth, later on, he was unable to maintain that monkhood in such a manner. In that context, abhijjhālū refers to one who has the nature of coveting others' property. Tibbasārāga refers to one with intense lust, either because it occurs constantly or because it is powerful. Byāpannacitta refers to one whose mind is corrupted by the state of putridity (due to anger). Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappa refers to one with a mind set on harming, like a rogue bull with sharp horns. Muṭṭhassati refers to one who is muddled in mindfulness, where an action done in one place disappears right there, like a crow that loses its mindfulness while looking at a meal served. Asampajāna refers to one without wisdom, lacking the knowledge that distinguishes the aggregates and so forth. Asamāhita refers to one with an unsettled mind, lacking access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), like a boat tied in a rough current. Vibbhantacitta refers to one with an agitated mind, like a deer caught in a snare. Pākatindriya refers to one with uncontrolled faculties, like a layman looking at his sons and daughters.

Chavālāta refers to a firebrand from a place where corpses are cremated. "Burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle" refers to a firebrand about eight finger-breadths long, burning at two ends and smeared with dung in the middle. "Not in the village" means that if that piece of wood could be taken for use as a yoke, a plow-pole, a rafter, or a bracket, it would serve a purpose for woodwork in the village. If it could be taken for use as a floorboard or a couch in a field-watchman's hut, it would serve a purpose for woodwork in the forest. Since it is useless in both places, it is spoken thus. "He falls away from the wealth of laypeople" means falling away from the benefits one would receive when laypeople living at home divide their inheritance. "The goal of monkhood" means failing to fulfill the goal of monkhood that should be attained through study (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha) by abiding in the instructions of teachers and preceptors. The Blessed One did not bring this simile for an immoral person (dussīla), but for a person who, though having pure virtue, is lazy and oppressed by faults such as covetousness.

Why was the statement "Monks, these three" undertaken? It was undertaken to show that this person's state of being like a firebrand (chavālāta) was not caused by parents, nor by teachers and preceptors, but was caused only by these evil, wrong thoughts. Or the signless...
279:
Concentration (samādhi) refers to insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi). That insight concentration is called signless concentration (animitta-samādhi) because it completely removes the signs of permanence and so forth. Among these foundations of mindfulness and signless concentration, the four foundations of mindfulness are a mixture of mundane and supramundane; signless concentration is a state occurring in the preliminary stage of the Path. Alternatively, it should be understood that signless concentration is the mixture, and the foundations of mindfulness occur in the preliminary stage of the Path.

The statement "Monks, these two views" was spoken to show that the development of signless concentration is not only for abandoning these three great thoughts, but also for the complete removal of the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) and the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). "Na vajjavā assa" means "I would be one without fault." The remaining words in this Pali text are clear. Thus, in this sutta as well, the Blessed One revolved the teaching through the three realms of existence and reached the pinnacle with Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, five hundred monks attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Pālileyyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "He set out on a journey" means that when the monks living in Kosambī were quarreling and disputing, the Blessed One one day brought up the story of King Dīghīti of Kosala and admonished them with verses such as "Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world." On that day, while those monks were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn. On the second day, the Blessed One told the same story again. On that day too, while they were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn. On the third day, the Blessed One told the same story again.

Then a certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One live without concern, devoted to dwelling happily in this very life. We will be known by this quarreling, disputing, strife, and contention." The Blessed One thought, "These foolish men have minds overwhelmed by defilements; it is not possible to make them understand." He then thought, "What benefit is there for me with these monks? I will live alone." Early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs and wandering for alms in Kosambī, the Blessed One set out on a journey alone, without a companion, without informing anyone.

The statement "Friends, at the time when" was spoken by the Elder Ānanda because he was expertly aware of all the Blessed One's movements. Whether the Blessed One would set out today with one monk, with two, with a hundred, with a thousand, or alone—all the Blessed One's manners were clear and evident to the Elder.
280:
“Anupubbena” means that while wandering for alms through villages and market towns in succession, the Buddha went to the village of Bālaka-loṇakāra, desiring to see a monk who was living in solitude. In that village of Bālaka-loṇakāra, he preached the benefits of solitary living throughout the afternoon and the three watches of the night to the Venerable Bhagu. The next day, after wandering for alms with that Elder as his attendant monk, he sent him back at that very place and, thinking, “I shall see the three noble sons who are living in harmony,” he went to the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park. To those noble sons as well, he preached the benefits of solitary living throughout the afternoon and the three watches of the night. Sending them back at that very place, he set out alone towards the city of Pāḷileyyaka and in due course arrived there. Therefore, it is said: “Wandering on tour in due course, he arrived at Pāḷileyyaka.”

“Bhaddasālamūle” means that the residents of Pāḷileyyaka, having offered alms to the Blessed One, built a leaf-hut for him in the Rakkhita forest grove not far from Pāḷileyyaka. Having obtained his consent with the request, “Please stay here,” they had him reside there. In that forest grove, there was a single, pleasant, and beautiful Sāla tree named “Bhaddasāla.” Depending on that city, the Blessed One stayed at the foot of that tree near the leaf-hut in that forest grove. Therefore, it is said: “At the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.”

While the Blessed One was staying there, a certain noble elephant, who was harassed by female elephants and calves in the grazing grounds and watering places, became weary of the herd. Thinking, “What benefit do I have from these elephants?” he left the herd and came to the path of humans. Seeing the Blessed One in the Pāḷileyyaka forest grove, he became cool and peaceful, like one whose fever is extinguished by a thousand jars of water, and stood in the presence of the Teacher. From that day on, the noble elephant performed major and minor duties for the Teacher, such as offering water for washing the face, bringing water for bathing, offering tooth-sticks, and sweeping the precinct. He brought sweet fruits of various kinds from the forest and offered them to the Teacher. The Teacher also partook of them (to encourage the elephant's faith).

One day, towards the end of the night, the Teacher, after walking in meditation, sat on a stone slab. The noble elephant also stood in a place not far away. When the Teacher looked behind, he saw nothing; likewise, when he looked in front and to both sides, he saw nothing. Then the thought occurred to the Teacher: “Indeed, I live happily, apart from those quarrelsome monks.” To the noble elephant also, the thought occurred: “There are no other elephants to eat the branches I have bent down,” and so on, thinking, “Indeed, happily...”
281:
“...I live alone, and I have the opportunity to perform duties for the Teacher.” The Teacher, having reflected on his own mind, thought: “Such a thought has arisen in me; I wonder what kind of thought has arisen in the noble elephant?” Seeing that the elephant's mind was the same, he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna):
“This mind of the noble elephant, the tusker,
Agrees with the mind [of the Buddha],
Since both delight in being alone in the forest.”

“Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū” means that while the Tathāgata was staying there in the Pāḷileyyaka forest, there were five hundred monks who had completed the rainy season residence in various directions. “Yenāyasmā Ānando” means that, thinking “The Teacher, it is said, has dismissed the Saṅgha of monks and entered the forest,” they did not dare to go to the Teacher's presence on their own, and so they approached the Venerable Ānanda.

“Anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo” refers to the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) which occurs immediately after the Path. “Vicayaso” means by means of investigation, through knowledge capable of investigating the nature of various phenomena. “Dhammo” refers to the Dhamma of the Dispensation (sāsana-dhamma). “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā” etc., refers to the various groups or categories into which the Dhamma was taught; this was said to manifest those categories. “Samanupassanā” refers to the observation of views (diṭṭhi-samanupassanā). “Saṅkhāro so” refers to that formation of view. “Tatojo so saṅkhāro” means that formation arises because of that craving. This arises even in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views among the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed. “Sāpi taṇhā” refers to that craving which is the cause of the formation of view. “Sāpi vedanā” refers to the feeling which is the cause of that craving. “So pi phasso” refers to the contact associated with ignorance which is the cause of feeling. “Sāpi avijjā” refers to the ignorance associated with that contact.

“No cassaṃ, no ca me siyā” means: If I were not, my requisites would not be. “Nābhavissaṃ, na me bhavissati” means: If in the future also I shall not be, thus because of my non-existence, my requisites also shall not be. In this place, the Blessed One taught according to the disposition of the person (puggalajjhāsaya) and the beauty of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa) in order to make that monk relinquish the view he had grasped. Regarding “Tatojo so saṅkhāro,” if it is asked: “How can the formation of doubt arise from craving when there is no doubt in the consciousness associated with craving?” [The answer is:] Because it has not been abandoned. For one who has not abandoned craving, that formation of doubt can arise. It is with reference to this meaning that this was said. The same method applies to views. Even though there is no associated view in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views, that view can arise because craving has not been abandoned. This meaning is appropriate with reference to the view of one who has not yet abandoned craving. In the manner already stated, in the ninth sutta, the Buddha taught insight (vipassanā) leading to the Fruit of Arahantship in twenty-three instances. The ninth sutta is finished.

In the tenth sutta, the words beginning with “Tadahuposathe” have already been explained in the Pavāraṇā Sutta. “Kiñcideva desaṃ” means a certain reason. [It refers to] when the Blessed One, staying in a state of admonishing, would ask questions. Why was this said? If those five hundred monks were to ask questions while the teacher was standing, and the student monks were sitting, it might show respect to the Blessed One but would be disrespectful to the teacher. If they were to stand up, it would be respectful to the teacher, but to the Blessed One...
282:
The volitional formation of doubt (vicikicchā-saṅkhāra) arises; with reference to that meaning, it is said: "tatojo so saṅkhāro" (that formation is born from that). In the case of wrong view (diṭṭhi) as well, this same method should be understood. Indeed, in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhigatavippayutta), there is no such thing as associated wrong view (sampayuttadiṭṭhi). However, because craving (taṇhā) has not yet been abandoned, that wrong view arises; therefore, with reference to the wrong view where craving is not yet abandoned, this meaning is appropriate even in those four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view. Thus, in this sutta, insight (vipassanā) leading to the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is taught in twenty-three places. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Puṇṇamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, the words beginning with "tadahuposathe" have already been explained in detail in the Pavāraṇa Sutta. "Kiဉ္ci deva desaṃ" means for some reason. Why did the Buddha say, "Sit in your own seat and ask when you wish"? That monk, it is said, had a retinue of five hundred monks. If the teacher were to ask while standing and those student monks remained seated, it would be a mark of respect toward the Teacher (the Buddha) but a mark of disrespect toward their own teacher. If they were to stand up, it would be a mark of respect toward their teacher but a mark of disrespect toward the Teacher (the Buddha). Thus, the minds of those student monks would become distracted and they would not be able to receive the teaching. Knowing that only when the teacher asks while seated would their minds be concentrated and able to receive the teaching, the Blessed One spoke in this way.

In the passage "Venerable Sir, these (aggregates) are," it should not be said that this Elder, despite being a group leader of five hundred monks, does not even know the five aggregates. A monk asking a question should not ask as if he already knows, thinking, "These five aggregates of clinging are not anything else"; therefore, he asks as if he does not know. Furthermore, he asks as if he does not know so that his students might think, "Our teacher does not say 'I know' [on his own], but speaks only after comparing with Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)," and thus consider the teaching worthy of listening to and believing.

"Chandamūlaka" means having desire-craving (taṇhā-chanda) as their root. Why did the Buddha say, "Bhikkhu, that clinging is not those five aggregates of clinging"? This was said because the five aggregates cannot be formed by mere desire and lust (chandarāga). However, because there is no clinging apart from the aggregates, whether by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) or by way of object (ārammaṇa), it was also said, "There is no clinging apart from the five aggregates of clinging."

When consciousness associated with craving is occurring, the matter (rūpa) produced by that consciousness is the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha); excluding that craving, the remaining four mental phenomena are the four mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha). Thus, even by way of co-nascence, there is no clinging apart from the aggregates. Since clinging arises by making one of the aggregates, such as matter, its object, there is no clinging apart from the five aggregates even by way of object. "Chandarāga-vemattatā" means the diversity or difference in desire and lust. "Bhikkhu, in this way" means that because of taking one of the aggregates like feeling as an object, a difference in the desire and lust directed toward the object of matter can occur.
283:
The diversity in desire and lust (chandarāga-vemattatā) can occur because of not taking one of the other aggregates, such as feeling, as an object. "Aggregate" (khandha) is the designation (paññatti) or name for the aggregates. Although this connection (anusandhi) might seem not to fit, even if it does not seem to fit, the question is indeed with connection, and the answer is also with connection. For this Elder asks according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those various monks, and the Teacher (the Buddha) also answers according to the inclinations of those various monks. The rest of the text is clear in all places. The tenth sutta is finished.

In each and every sutta of this chapter (vagga), five hundred monks each reached the fruit of Arahantship.
