## 9. Thera Vagga

## 1. Ānandasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Thera Vagga, "Mantāṇiputta" means the son of the Brahmin woman named Mantāṇī. "Upādāya" means depending on, starting from, with reference to, or grasping. The three proliferations (papañca) of craving, conceit, and wrong view, which occur as "I am" (asmi), arise. "Dahara" means a young person. "Yuvā" means one endowed with the prime of youth. "Maṇḍanakajātika" means one who has the nature or habit of adorning oneself. "Mukhanimitta" means the reflection of the face. That reflection of the face appears depending on a pure mirror-circle. Does the person looking into that mirror see his own face or another's face? If it were his own, it should appear as if facing away. If it were another's, it should appear as being different in color and so on. Therefore, they say that the reflection is neither one's own nor another's, but is merely a reflected form (nibhāsarūpa) that appears depending on the mirror. As for why a reflection appears in water, it is because of the purity of the great elements (mahābhūta). "I have realized the Dhamma" means "I have realized the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths through knowledge; I have become a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)." The first sutta is finished.
284:
## 2. Tissasuttavaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "madhurakajāto viya" means being heavy and sluggish in body and unfit for activity, like someone who has eaten sweet food. "Disāpi me" means "This is the East, this is the South"—in this way, the directions are not clearly perceived by me. "Dhammāpi maṃ na paṭibhanti" means the scriptures (pariyatti) that have been learned and recited do not appear clearly to me; I no longer see what has been learned. "Vicikicchā" does not refer to the sixteen types of great doubt about whether the Dispensation (sāsana) leads out of suffering. For that man of good birth, it is only the doubt: "Will I be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, or will I only be able to manage carrying the bowl and robes?"

In the phrase "kāmānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ," for example, to someone looking at a deep pond, there is delight just in seeing it, but fierce fish pull down and destroy anyone who enters that pond. Similarly, in the five cords of sensual pleasure, there is only delight in the objects of the eye-door and so on, but they pull down those who are greedy for those sensual pleasures into hell and other such states. Because sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and great despair, and because the danger in them is excessive, it is said, "This is a designation for sensual pleasures," based on this special reason. "Ahamanuggahena" means "I, the Buddha, will support him with the support of Dhamma and the support of material requisites." "Abhinandī" means accepting well. Not only did he accept it, but having obtained such relief from the Teacher and by striving and exerting himself, he was established in the fruit of Arahatship within a few days. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Yamakasuttavaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "diṭṭhigataṃ" means if that monk Yamaka had perceived, "Formations arise and cease; only the process of formations becomes a non-process," it would not be a wrong view but would be knowledge occurring within the Dispensation. However, because he held the view, "A being is annihilated and destroyed," it became a wrong view. "Thāmasā parāmasā" means by the strength of the view and by the misapprehension of the view.

"Yenāyasmā Sāriputto" means, for example, when an uprising occurs in a border region and the royal officers are unable to suppress it, they go to the general or the king. Similarly, when the Elder Yamaka was in an "uprising" through his wrong view, those monks, being unable to calm that wrong view, approached the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma of the King of Dhamma. "Evaṃbyā kho" means that because he did not dare to confirm and speak his view in the presence of the Elder Sāriputta as he did in the presence of those monks, he spoke "Evaṃbyā kho" with a dejected heart.
285:
Those monks approached the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. The phrase "evaṃbyā kho" means that because he was unable to speak firmly by upholding his view in the presence of the Great Elder as he did in the presence of those monks, he said "evaṃbyā kho" with a hanging (dejected) heart. "What do you think, friend Yamaka?"—the Elder Sāriputta, having heard those words of the Elder Yamaka, thought, "This Yamaka does not yet see the fault in his own view; I will make that fault clear through a Dhamma teaching," and began to teach the Dhamma with three cycles.

Why was this started: "What do you think, friend Yamaka, is form the Tathāgata (a being)?" It was to make him perform the duty of investigation. Indeed, at the end of the three-cycle teaching, the Elder became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). After that, to make the Elder Yamaka perform the duty of investigation, he said, "What do you think?" and so on. "Tathāgata" here means a being (satta). He asks, "Do you see the Tathāgata (a being) by combining these five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?" In the phrase "ettha ca te, āvuso," this is the locative case used in the Elder's investigation. This is what is meant: In this matter, even in the present life, a being cannot be found truly or permanently. "If, friend, you [were asked]"—this is asked because he wished to have Yamaka declare the fruit of Arahatship. The meaning is that he should answer: "Whatever is suffering, that alone has ceased; there is no being other than suffering that is subject to cessation."

"For this very purpose" means for the sake of this first path. "For knowledge of exceeding measure" means for the sake of knowledge of an extraordinary amount, and for the manifestation of the three higher paths along with insight (vipassanā). "Endowed with protection" means being possessed of both internal and external protection. "Desiring what is not secure" means not desiring the state of security from the four yokes (bonds). "Pasayha" means by oppressing and overcoming. "Anupakhajja" means by entering closely.

In the terms "one who rises first" and so on, one is called "pubbuṭṭhāyī" because, upon seeing someone coming from afar, one rises from one's seat first. Because one gives a seat to that person and then lies down or sits after that person has sat, one is called "pacchānipātī." Alternatively, one is called "pubbuṭṭhāyī" because one rises earliest in the morning and manages, saying, "This many of you go to plow, this many of you go to sow." One is also called "pacchānipātī" because in the evening, when everyone has gone to their respective dwellings, one arranges protection around the house, closes the doors, and lies down last of all. "What..."
286:
"Sir, what shall I do? Sir, what shall I do?"—because he looks at the face and knows what task is to be done, he is called a 'kiሐkārapaቩissāvĩ' (one who responds to what is to be done). Because he acts in a pleasing way, he is called a 'manāpacārĩ'. Because he speaks endearing words, he is called a 'piyavādĩ'. Because he should be trusted as "This person is my good friend," he is called a 'mitta' (friend). Because he would become intimate by drinking and eating together, it is said 'vissāsaሐ āpajjeyya' (entering into intimacy). 'Saሐvissattha' means being very intimate.

"Evameva kho" (In the same way): In this phrase, the comparison with this simile should be understood. The uninstructed worldling, while dependent on the round of rebirth, is like the foolish son of a householder. The five weak aggregates are like the murderous enemy. The five aggregates that have arrived at the moment of rebirth are like the murderous enemy who approached saying, "I will serve the householder's son." Just as there is a time when that householder's son does not know, "This is not my friend, this is a murderous enemy," so too should be understood the time when the worldling dependent on the round does not grasp the five aggregates as "These are not mine," but grasps them as "My form, my feeling, my perception, my mental formations, my consciousness." Just as there is a time when one treats the murderer with honor, grasping him as "This is my friend," so too should be understood the time when one cares for the five aggregates by bathing and feeding them, grasping them as "These are mine." Just as the murderer cuts off the head with a sword while being honored, after knowing "This person is very intimate with me," so too should be understood the ending of life for the intimate foolish worldling by the aggregates that are sharply breaking apart.

'Upeti' means approaches. 'Upādiyati' means takes. 'Adhiቩቩhāti' means establishes by way of superior attention. 'Attā me' means "This form is my self." "But, friends, the instructed noble disciple" (sutavā ca kho āvuso ariyasāvako) means: just as a wise householder's son, knowing such an approaching enemy as "This is my enemy," is not heedless, makes him perform various tasks, avoids misfortune, and reaches prosperity; so too the instructed noble disciple, by the method of "not regarding form as self," etc., does not cling to the five aggregates as "I" or "mine," but knowing "These five aggregates are my enemies," applies insight (vipassanā) by way of the heptad of form (rũpasattaka), the heptad of the formless (arũpasattaka), etc., avoids the suffering caused by those aggregates, and reaches the supreme fruit, Arahantship. The remaining words in this sutta are clear. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Anurādhasutta-vaሔሔanā

In the fourth sutta, "araሑሑakuቩikāyaሐ" (in a forest hut) means in a leaf-roofed hut at the edge of that same monastery. "Taሐ tathāgato" means the Buddha, who is your teacher, that Tathāgata...
287:
...the being, the Tathāgata. Regarding the phrase "other than these," it is said that the Elder Anurādha had this thought: "These people are opponents and enemies of the Dispensation. Our teacher, the Buddha, will not designate as these people say; he will designate in another way." Therefore, he spoke thus. When this was said, those of other sects—even though the Elder spoke without knowing his own doctrine or the doctrine of others, those wanderers of other sects, who knew the doctrine of the Dispensation in part and wished to find fault in the Elder's argument, said this to the Venerable Anurādha.

"Anurādha, what do you think?" and so forth. The Buddha, having heard the Elder Anurādha's words, thought: "This monk does not yet know the fault in his own view. However, he is a practitioner, one who is devoted to effort. I will make him understand through the Dhamma teaching alone." Wishing to teach the discourse with the three-fold round (tiparivaቩቩa), he said, "Anurādha, what do you think?" and so forth. Then, wishing to assign the practice of application (anuyogavatta) to that Elder who had reached Arahantship through that teaching, he said, "Anurādha, what do you think? Do you regard form as the Tathāgata?" and so forth. In the phrase "I designate only suffering and the cessation of suffering," he designates the suffering of the round (vaቩቩa) and Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the suffering of the round. Alternatively, by the word "suffering," the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) is taken. When that is taken, the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) is also taken because it is its root. By the word "cessation," the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is taken. When that is taken, the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) is also taken because it is the means (upāya). Thus he shows, "Anurādha, formerly and now, I designate only the Four Noble Truths." Thus, in this sutta, only the round (vaቩቩa) and the ending of the round (vivaቩቩa) are discussed. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Vakkalisutta-vaሔሔanā

In the fifth sutta, "kumbhakāranivesane" (in the potter's house) means in the potter's workshop. It is said that Elder Vakkali, after completing the rains retreat and performing the invitation (pavāraሔā), was coming to see the Blessed One. A severe illness arose for that Elder in the middle of the city, and his feet could no longer carry his body. Then, they carried him to the potter's hall on a small litter. That hall was their workshop, not a residential house. Referring to that workshop, it is said, "He dwells in the potter's house." "Bāሷhagilāno" (gravely ill) means being intensely ill. "Samadhosi" (lowered) means lowering down from all sides; it shows respect through a moving gesture. It is said to be a duty that even a person who is gravely ill, upon seeing one who is more senior, should show respect by the gesture of rising. When doing so, the senior person should say, "Do not move, do not move." "These seats exist" means that in the time of the Buddha, even for a single monk...
288:
In the place where the monks reside, it is customary to prepare a seat, even if it is just a wooden plank or a spread of leaves, with the intention: "If the Teacher comes, he will sit here." The phrase "khamanīyaṃ yāpanīyaṃ" refers to asking whether one is able to endure suffering or whether one is able to maintain the postures (iriyāpatha). "Paṭikkamanti" means receding or decreasing. "Abhikkamanti" means advancing or increasing. "Paṭikkamosānaṃ" means having the end of the receding of those feelings. "Sīlato na upavadati" means that one does not reproach oneself regarding virtue, by virtue of being virtuous. "Cirapaṭikāhaṃ" means "I, since a long time ago." Regarding "pūtikāyena" (with this foul body), the Blessed One spoke thus even of his own golden-hued body because of its nature of constant oozing. In the statement "Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me," the Blessed One shows the nature of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāyatā), as it was said: "Great King, the Tathāgata is indeed the Dhamma-body." Indeed, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is called the body of the Tathāgata.

Now, wishing to begin the threefold cycle of Dhamma teaching to the Elder, he said "Taṃ kiṃ maññasi" and so forth. "Kāḷasilā" refers to the Kāḷasilā Monastery. "Vimokkhāya" means for the sake of the liberation of the path (magga-vimokkha). "Suvimutto vimuccissati" means that having been liberated through the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, he will be liberated. Those deities, knowing that "this monk has begun insight (vipassanā) in this manner and will reach Arahantship without obstacle," spoke thus. "Apāpakaṃ" means not inferior (noble). "He took the weapon" means that the Elder was formerly an "adhimānika" person (one with overestimation) who thought he had attained Arahantship. That Elder, not seeing the manifestation of defilements that were suppressed by concentration and insight, perceived "I am an Arahant," and thinking, "What is the use of this painful life to me? I will die by killing myself with a weapon," he cut his throat with a sharp weapon. At that moment, intense painful feelings arose in the Elder. In that instant, realizing he was only a worldling (puthujjana), and because his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) was not abandoned, he quickly took up his original meditation subject, contemplated it, and attained Arahantship just as he passed away (attained Parinibbāna). If it is asked how his reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) occurred: although it is not the case that every Arahant must necessarily obtain all nineteen reviewing knowledges, even while the head is being cut by a sharp sword, one or two thought-processes (vīthi) of knowledge certainly arise.

"Vivattakkhandhaṃ" means having a body that has turned over. "Semānaṃ" means sleeping (or reclining). The Elder took the weapon while reclining on his back. Although his body remained as it was, his head turned to the right side and stayed there. Noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) mostly pass away while leaning on their right side. Therefore, while the body was on its back, the head turned to the right; referring to this, it is called "vivattakkhandha." "Dhūmāyitattaṃ" means...
289:
"Dhūmāyitattaṃ" means the state of smoking. "Timirāyitattaṃ" means the state of being dark and gloomy like a dark cloud. The meaning is: like a cloud of smoke or like a cloud of darkness. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Assajisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "Kassapakārāme" means in the monastery built by the wealthy merchant Kassapa. "Kāya-saṅkhāra" refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths. The Elder Assaji used to dwell having calmed them through the fourth jhāna. "Evaṃ hoti" means that now, to the Elder Assaji who does not regain that concentration, such a thought occurs. He thought: "Will I not fall away from the Dispensation (Sāsana)?" Due to the fault of his illness, his attained meditative attainments (samāpatti) had declined; therefore, he thought thus. "Samādhisārakā samādhisāmaññā" refers to those who consider concentration alone as the essence and as the state of a recluse. But in my Dispensation, this concentration is not the essence; insight, the paths, and the fruits are the essence. Why do you, while falling away from concentration, think "I am falling away from the Dispensation"? After reassuring the Elder, the Buddha began the threefold cycle of Dhamma teaching with "Taṃ kiṃ maññasi" and so forth. Then, showing the constant dwelling of the Elder Assaji who reached Arahantship at the end of the threefold teaching, he said "So sukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati" and so forth. In that text, regarding "anabhinanditā'ti pajānāti": if it is asked, "Let there be delight in pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) first, but how can there be delight in painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā)?"—when one reaches pain, one longs for pleasure. To the extent that one longs for pleasure, to that extent one longs for pain. Because through the change of pleasure, pain inevitably comes. Thus, delight in pain should be understood. The rest of the words are as previously explained. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Khemakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "Attaniya" means one's own belongings or requisites. "Asmī'ti adhigataṃ" means the attainment of craving and conceit that occur as "I am." "Sandhāvanikāyā" means by going and coming repeatedly. "Upasaṅkami" means he went from the Badarikārāma Monastery to the Ghositārāma Monastery, which was about a gāvuta (approx. 2 miles) away. Dāsaka Thera traveled a distance of about two leagues (yojana) that day by going back and forth four times. Why did the elders send Dāsaka Thera? Because they wished to hear the Dhamma from a renowned Dhamma-preacher. Why did the elders themselves not go? The place where the Elder resided was a forest and very cramped; there was no space for sixty elders to stand or sit, so they did not go. "Coming here, to us, the Dhamma..."
290:
Why did they not send a message saying "Please preach"? Because the Elder was ill. Then why did they send messages repeatedly? Thinking, "He will come to preach to us once he knows [our intention] for himself." The Elder, knowing their intention, indeed went.

"Friends, I do not [say] 'I am' regarding form" means: If a person says "I am" regarding form alone, he rejects the other four mental aggregates. If a person says [it] regarding aggregates other than form, he rejects form. The same method applies to feeling and so on. For the Elder, however, the conceit "I am" (asmi-māna) was found in the five aggregates as a whole; therefore, he spoke thus. "Hoteva" means "hoti yeva" (it indeed is). "Anusahagata" means subtle. "Ūsa" means alkaline salt from wood-ash. "Khāra" means alkaline salt. "Sammadditvā" means soaking and letting [the salt] eat away [the dirt].

In the phrase "In this very way," there is this comparison: The mental continuum of a worldling (puthujjana) should be understood as a soiled cloth. The three contemplations (anupassanā) should be understood as the three alkaline salts. The mental continuum of a non-returner (anāgāmī), which remains after being processed by the teaching, should be understood as a cloth washed with the three salts. The defilements to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship should be understood as the subtle smell of wood-ash salt and so on. The knowledge of the path of Arahatship should be understood as a scent box. The destruction of all defilements by the path of Arahatship should be understood as the complete removal of the subtle smell of wood-ash salt by relying on the scent box. The conduct of an Arahat whose taints are destroyed, wandering as he pleases while spreading the fragrance of virtue (sīla) and so on to the ten directions, should be understood as a youth with a fragrant scent wandering on the main street on a festival day wearing a cloth permeated with perfume.

"Ācikkhituṃ" means to describe. "Desetuṃ" means to show clearly. "Paññāpetuṃ" means to make known. "Paṭṭhapetuṃ" means to establish. "Vivarituṃ" means to open or reveal. "Vibhajituṃ" means to analyze well. "Uttānīkātuṃ" means to make plain. "The sixty Elders" means: those Elders developed insight (vipassanā) at every point the Elder [Khemaka] preached, and by investigating stage by stage, they attained Arahatship at the conclusion of the teaching. The Elder also preached not by any other method but with a mind joined with insight. Therefore, he too attained Arahatship. Thus it is said: "The minds of the sixty Elders and the Venerable Khemaka were liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging." The seventh sutta is finished.
291:
## 8. Channasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "Venerable Channa" was one born on the same day as the Tathāgata and went forth together with him on the day of the Great Renunciation. Later, he was ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. He was an Elder who used to offend his fellow practitioners with harsh speech, being full of disparaging (makkha) and domineering (paḷāsa) qualities, saying "Our Buddha, our Dhamma." "Avāpuraṇaṃ ādāya" means taking the key. "Vihārena vihāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā" means entering one monastery and then approaching other monasteries in succession from there. Why did he go to those places with such great effort and speak thus, saying "Please admonish me"? It was because of the arising of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). For after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Venerable Ānanda, sent by the senior Elders who were the compilers of the Dhamma led by Mahākassapa, went to Kosambī and imposed the Brahmadaṇḍa (the supreme penalty). When that Brahmadaṇḍa was imposed, he was greatly distressed and fainted. Upon regaining consciousness, he stood up and went to a monk, but that monk did not say a single word to him. He went to another, but he too did not speak. Thus, after wandering through the entire monastery and becoming weary, he took his bowl and robes and went to Vārāṇasī. Having developed spiritual urgency, he went to various monasteries and spoke in this manner.

"All formations are impermanent" means all formations belonging to the three planes are impermanent. "All things are non-self" means all things belonging to the four planes are non-self. Thus, when all those monks admonished the Elder, they spoke only of the two marks—the mark of impermanence and the mark of non-self—and did not speak of the mark of suffering. Why did they not speak of it? It is said they had this thought: "This monk is loose-tongued; if the mark of suffering is pointed out, saying 'Form is suffering... consciousness is suffering, the Path is suffering, the Fruit is suffering,' he might take it wrongly, thinking 'You are just monks who have reached suffering.'" Intending to teach him in a faultless way so that he could not take it wrongly, they spoke only of the two marks.

"Paritassanā upādānaṃ uppajjati" means anxiety and clinging arise. "The mind recoils, then what is my self?" means: if not even one of these things like form is self, then what indeed is my self? Thus his mind recoiled from the insight he was practicing. It is said that this Elder began insight without grasping the causes (paccaya); therefore, that weak insight, being unable to overcome the clinging to self, appeared [to him] as voidness in formations.
292:
When conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) appear as empty of self and what belongs to self, it becomes a cause for the arising of the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and anxiety (paritassanā), thinking, "I shall be annihilated, I shall perish." Seeing himself like one falling off a cliff, the Elder Channa said, "Anxiety and grasping arise, the mind recoils; if so, who is my self now?" The phrase "For one who sees such Dhamma, this does not happen" means that for one who sees the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, such a way of thinking does not occur. "That much intimacy" refers to that much confidence or familiarity. Hearing the words, "This Dhamma has appeared before me," the Elder Ānanda, considering "What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for this person?", searched through the Buddha's words in the Tipiṭaka and saw the Kaccānagotta Sutta. Thinking, "This Sutta untangles the entanglement of wrong views at the very beginning, shows the power of the Buddha in the middle, and explains the subtle nature of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda); I shall preach this Sutta," he spoke the words starting with "Sammukhā metaṃ." The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9-10. Rāhulasuttādivaṇṇanā
91-92. The ninth and tenth suttas have the same meaning as those already preached in the Rāhula Saṃyutta. They are included here simply because this is the Thera Vagga. The ninth and tenth suttas are finished.

## Thera Vagga the Ninth.

## 10. Puppha Vagga

## 1. Nadīsuttavaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Puppha Vagga, "pabbateyyā" refers to rivers that originate and flow from mountains. "Ohārinī" refers to a river that carries downstream things like grass, leaves, and wood that have fallen into the current. "Dūraṅgamā" refers to a river that travels a long distance, about four or five hundred yojanas from its starting point. "Sīghasotā" refers to a river with a swift current. "Kāsa" and others refer to all types of grasses. "Rukkhā" refers to weak trees such as the castor-oil plant. "Te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ" means that although those trees grow on the bank, they would hang over or lean over the water with their tips touching it. "Palujjeyyuṃ" means they would fall onto the head along with the roots and clods of earth. That person, being overwhelmed by those roots and earth, would reach great destruction due to the sand, mud, and water entering the mouth.
293:
In the phrase "Evameva kho," the foolish worldling (bāla-puthujjana) who relies on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) should be understood as the man who has fallen into the current. The weak five aggregates should be understood as the kāsa grass and others on both banks of the river. Just as that man unknowingly grasps those grasses although they cannot save him, the foolish worldling's grasping of the aggregates with the four kinds of grasping (upādāna), without knowing that "these aggregates are not my companions," should be understood. Just as the man reaches destruction because the grasped grasses break away, the foolish worldling's reaching of destruction such as sorrow when the aggregates grasped with the four kinds of grasping undergo change and perish should be understood. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Pupphasuttavaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "vivadati" (disputes) means arguing by speaking falsely as "permanent, happy, self, and beautiful" against one who speaks according to the true nature as "impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul." "Lokadhammo" refers to the group of the five aggregates. Because they have the nature of disintegrating (lujjana), they are called "loka." "Kinti karomi" means "What shall I do?" It shows that the Buddha's responsibility is only to preach the practice (paṭipatti), while fulfilling the practice is the responsibility of the sons of good family. In this sutta, the three worlds are preached. In the passage "Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, lokena," the world of beings (satta-loka) is preached. In the passage "Atthi, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo," the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka) is preached. In the passage "Tathāgato loke jāto loke saṃvaḍḍho," the world of locations (okāsa-loka) is preached. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Pheṇapiṇḍūpamasuttavaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "Gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre" (on the bank of the river Ganges) means that the people of Ayojjhā, seeing the Tathāgata arriving at their city while wandering for alms accompanied by an immeasurable company of monks, built a monastery for the Teacher in a place adorned with a large forest grove at a bend in the Ganges and offered it. The Blessed One resided there. With reference to that monastery, it is said, "Gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre." "Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi" means that the Blessed One, residing in that monastery, came out of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) in the evening and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared on the bank of the Ganges. Seeing a large lump of foam (pheṇapiṇḍa) floating down the river Ganges, he thought, "I shall preach a Dhamma related to the five aggregates in my Dispensation," and addressed the monks who were sitting around him.
294:
“Mahantaṃ pheṇapiṇḍaṃ” refers to a great lump of foam of such a nature that, starting from the size of a ripe jujube fruit at its place of origin, it gradually grows as it floats down with the current until it becomes the size of a mountain peak, serving as a dwelling place for many creatures such as water snakes. “Āvaheyya” means it would carry or bring along. That lump of foam may break at its place of origin, or after traveling a short distance, or after traveling a distance of one or two leagues. Even if it does not break in the interim, it will certainly break upon reaching the great ocean. “Nijjhāyeyya” means one would look at it intently. “Yoniso upaparikkheyya” means one would investigate and reflect by way of cause. “Monks, what essence could there be in a lump of foam?” means, monks, what could be called an essence in a lump of foam? There can be none; it merely dissolves and perishes.

“Evameva kho” means just as a lump of foam is without essence, so too, form (rūpa) is without essence because it is devoid of permanent essence (nicca-sāra), stable essence (dhuva-sāra), and self-essence (atta-sāra). Just as that lump of foam cannot be taken with the thought, “I will make a bowl or a saucer with this,” and even if taken by some means, it cannot fulfill that purpose and only breaks; so too, form cannot be taken as “permanent,” “stable,” “I,” or “mine.” Even if it is taken as such, it does not remain so, but is only of the nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness. Thus, it is just like a lump of foam. Alternatively, just as a lump of foam is full of holes and apertures, composed of many joints, and is the home of many creatures like water snakes; so too, form is full of holes and apertures, composed of many joints, and is the dwelling place of eighty families of worms. That very collection of form is their birth-house, their toilet, their infirmary, and their cemetery. These worms do not go elsewhere but perform their birthing and so on right in this body. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam.

Just as a lump of foam, which is initially the size of a ripe jujube fruit, gradually becomes as large as a mountain peak; so too, form, which is initially just the kalala-liquid, gradually becomes a fathom in length in the case of humans, the size of a mountain peak in the case of cattle, buffaloes, elephants, etc., and a size of many hundreds of leagues in the case of fish, turtles, etc. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam. Just as a lump of foam breaks as soon as it arises, or after going a little way, or after going a long way, but certainly breaks upon reaching the ocean; so too, form breaks even in the kalala stage, or in the abbuda stage and so on. Even if it does not break in the interim, for those with a hundred-year lifespan, it certainly breaks upon reaching a hundred years. In the mouth of Death, it reaches utter destruction. In this way too, it is like a lump of foam.
295:
In the words “Monks, what essence could there be in feeling?” and so on, the similarity of feeling and the other aggregates to a water bubble and so on should be understood. Just as a water bubble is without essence, so too is feeling. Just as that water bubble is weak and cannot be grasped—it is not possible to take that water bubble and make a plank or a seat, and even if grasped, it only breaks—so too, feeling is weak and cannot be grasped; it cannot be grasped as “permanent” or “stable.” Even if grasped, it does not remain so. Because of this quality of being ungraspable, feeling is like a water bubble. Furthermore, just as a water bubble arises and breaks at each and every drop of water and does not last long, so too, feeling arises and breaks and does not last long. Within the duration of a finger-snap, it arises and ceases hundreds of thousands of millions of times. Just as a water bubble arises depending on four causes—the water surface, a drop of water, water impurity, and the trapping of air—so too, feeling arises depending on four causes: the base (vatthu), the object (ārammaṇa), the impurity of defilements (kilesa-jalla), and the impact of contact (phassa). In this way too, feeling is like a water bubble.

Perception (saññā) is also like a mirage in the sense of being essenceless. Similarly, it is like a mirage in the sense of being ungraspable. It is not possible to take that mirage to drink, to bathe, or to fill a vessel. Furthermore, just as a mirage flickers and appears like the surge of waves, so too, perception, with its divisions such as the perception of blue, flickers and moves for the purpose of experiencing objects like blue. Just as a mirage deceives the multitude, making them say, “It looks like a lake full of water, like a river full of water,” so too, perception deceives, making one say, “This object is blue, it is beautiful, it is pleasant, it is permanent.” The same method applies to yellow and so on. In this way, because of its deceptive nature, perception is like a mirage.

“Akukkukajātaṃ” refers to that which has not yet grown a solid, hard core inside. Volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are also like a plantain trunk in the sense of being essenceless. Similarly, they are like a plantain trunk in the sense of being ungraspable for use. Just as it is not possible to take anything from a plantain trunk to use for rafters and so on, and even if used, it does not serve that purpose; so too, volitional formations cannot be grasped by way of permanence and so on, and even if grasped, they do not become so. Just as a plantain trunk is a combination of many layers of sheaths, so too, the aggregate of volitional formations is a combination of many states. Just as a plantain trunk has various characteristics—the color of the outer sheath being one kind, and the colors of the successive inner sheaths being different—so too...
296:
In the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the characteristic of contact (phassa) is one thing, and the characteristics of volition (cetanā) and so forth are another; however, when combined, they are simply called the aggregate of mental formations. Thus, the aggregate of mental formations is like a plantain trunk.

A man with vision refers to one who is endowed with both the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu). His fleshly eye should be pure, free from cataracts and diseases, and his wisdom eye should be capable of seeing the coreless nature [of things]. Consciousness (viññāṇa) is like an illusion (māyā) because it is coreless and because it is useless. Just as an illusion is transient and appears quickly, so is consciousness. Indeed, it is even more transient and appears even more quickly than that. It is because of this mind that a man appears as if he has come, as if he has gone, as if he is standing, or as if he is sitting. In reality, the mind at the time of coming is one, and the mind at the time of going and so forth is another. Thus, consciousness is like an illusion.

Just as an illusion deceives the masses, making them perceive something as "this is gold, silver, or pearl," so consciousness deceives the masses. By that very mind, it makes them perceive one as if coming, going, standing, or sitting. The mind in coming is one, and the mind in going and so forth is another. Thus, consciousness is like an illusion.

Bhūripaññena means having subtle wisdom and vast, extensive wisdom. Āyu is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). Usmā is the heat born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu). Parabhattaṃ means becoming the food for various kinds of worms and so forth. This kind of continuity remains with the corpse until it reaches the cemetery. Māyāyaṃ bālālāpinī refers to the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), which is called the art of illusion that causes the foolish masses to lament, "I, mine." Vadhaka (murderer) refers to the aggregates being called murderers for two reasons: because they destroy one another, and because when the aggregates exist, killing and so forth become manifest.

When the single earth element breaks, it breaks taking the remaining elements with it; likewise with the water element and so forth. When the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) breaks, it breaks taking the mental aggregates with it. Among the mental aggregates, feeling (vedanā) and so forth break taking perception (saññā) and so forth with them. These four mental aggregates also break taking the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) with them. Thus, their nature as murderers should be understood through this mutual destruction. Furthermore, when the aggregates exist, killing, binding, and cutting can occur; thus, their nature as murderers should also be understood from the fact that they are the cause of such acts. Sabbasaṃyogaṃ refers to all ten fetters (saṃyojana). Accutaṃ padaṃ refers to Nibbāna. The third sutta is finished.
297:
## 4-6. Commentary on the Gomayapiṇḍa Sutta, etc.

96-98. In the fourth sutta, "sassatisamaṃ" means lasting as long as eternal things such as Mount Sineru, the earth, the moon, and the sun. "Parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍaṃ" refers to a small lump of cow-dung the size of a madhuka flower. Where was this lump of cow-dung obtained? Some say it was picked up from what was brought for smearing [the floor]. In truth, it should be understood that it was created by psychic power and placed on the palm of the hand to make the meaning clear. "Attabhāvapāṭilābho" refers to the obtained individual existence (body). "Na yidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha" means that the practice of this noble life, the Path, would not be evident. This is because the Path arises by overturning the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) within the three realms. If even an individual existence as small as this lump of cow-dung were permanent, the Path, even if it arose, would not be able to overturn the cycle of formations; therefore, the practice of the holy life would not be evident.

Now, to show that "if any formation were permanent, the prosperity I enjoyed during the time of King Mahāsudassana would also be permanent, but even that prosperity was impermanent," he said, "In the past, bhikkhus, I was a king," and so forth. In that text, "Kusāvatī-rājadhāni-ppamukhāni" means that the royal city of Kusāvatī was the chief and most excellent among those cities. "Sāramayāni" means [couches] made of the heartwood of red sandalwood. However, the pillows of all those couches were made only of cloth woven with thread. "Goṇakatthatāni" means [couches] spread with black rugs having hair longer than four finger-breadths, which are also called wide-backed rugs. "Paṭakatthatāni" means [couches] spread with white blankets made of wool with hair on both sides. "Paṭalikatthatāni" means [couches] spread with woolen coverings densely embroidered with flowers. "Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni" means [couches] spread with excellent coverings made of the hide of the kadali antelope. It is said that these coverings are made by spreading and sewing the kadali antelope hide over white cloth. "Sauttaracchadāni" means [couches] together with a red canopy fastened above. "Ubhatolohitakūpadhānāni" means couches having red pillows at both ends, for the head and for the feet. In the phrase "Vejayantarathappamukhāni", Vejayanta is the name of that king's chariot. The hubs of its wheels were made of sapphire (indanīla), the spokes were made of the seven gems, the rims were made of coral, the axle was made of silver, the body (upakkhara) was made of sapphire, and the pole (kubbara) was made of silver. That chariot was the chief and best among all chariots. "Dukūlasandānāni" means [chariots] having floor-coverings made of dukūla cloth. "Kaṃsūpadharaṇāni" means [cows] having milking vessels made of silver. "Vatthakoṭisahassāni" means...
298:
"He will enjoy as he pleases"—this was said with reference only to the change of clothes offered while he stood after bathing. "Bhattābhihāro" means the meal-offering brought along with an escort.

"At that time, I dwelt in such a city"—this refers to only the one city where he resided. In the other cities, his sons, daughters, and servant-folk lived. The same principle applies to the palaces and gabled chambers. Among the couches and so forth, he personally used only one, while the rest were for the use of his children and others. Among the queens, only one attended to him, while the others were merely a retinue. "Velāmika" refers to a queen born from the womb of a Khattiya and a Brāhmaṇī, or a Brāhmaṇa and a Khattiyā princess. "He wears" means he wears only one pair of garments, and it is shown that the remaining garments are for the one million, six hundred and eighty thousand attendants who follow him. "He eats" means he eats at most only one measure (nāḷika) of rice, and it is shown that the rest is for the eight hundred and forty thousand attendants who follow him. This is because one pot of rice is sufficient for ten people.

Having thus shown the prosperity during the time of King Mahāsudassana, the Buddha now said, "Thus, bhikkhus..." and so forth, wishing to show the impermanence of that prosperity. In that text, "vipariṇatā" means having reached a state beyond designation, like an extinguished lamp, by abandoning its natural state. "Bhikkhus, thus saṅkhāras are impermanent" means they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. With these words, the Blessed One descended as if a man were to set up a ladder against a Campaka tree a hundred cubits high, climb it, take a Campaka flower, and then let go of the ladder to descend. Similarly, as if setting up a ladder, he ascended to the prosperity of Mahāsudassana, which was more than hundreds of thousands of crores of years high, and then, taking hold of the characteristic of impermanence at the peak of that prosperity, he descended as if letting go of the ladder. Thus, they are "impermanent" (adhuvā) because they lack stability like water bubbles, and they are "without relief" (anassāsikā) because they provide no comfort, like drinking water or being anointed with sandalwood in a dream. Thus, the characteristic of impermanence is taught in this sutta. In the fifth sutta, everything is as previously explained. The sixth sutta was taught according to the disposition of one who could understand in that way. The fourth and subsequent suttas are finished.

## 7. Gaddulabaddhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "the great ocean" refers to the time when the great ocean dries up upon the rising of the fifth sun. "Making an end of suffering" means the ending of the suffering of the round for beings who are shrouded by ignorance and have not penetrated the Four Noble Truths...
299:
...I do not speak of a limit (to the suffering of the round). "Sā gaddulabaddho" means like a dog bound by a leash. "Khīle" refers to a large stake driven into the earth. "Thambhe" refers to a pillar that has been buried. In this analogy, the fool who relies on the round of rebirth is like the dog; wrong view (diṭṭhi) is like the leash; and self-identity (sakkāya) is like the pillar. Just as a dog bound to a pillar by a leash merely circles around that pillar, it should be understood that the worldling, bound to self-identity by the leash of craving and wrong view, merely wanders around self-identity. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Dutiya-gaddulabaddhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "tasmā" (therefore) means: because the foolish worldling, who relies on the round and is bound to the pillar of self-identity by the rope of craving accompanied by wrong view, exists in all postures only by relying on the five aggregates; or, because this mind has for a long time been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion, therefore (this was said). "Defilement of mind" (cittasံkilesā) means that even if beings are well-bathed and clean, they are defiled only because of the defilement of the mind; even if their bodies are covered in dirt, they are pure because of the purity of the mind. Therefore, the ancients said:

"The Great Sage did not say: 'When form is defiled, beings are defiled; when form is pure, beings are pure.'

But the Great Sage did say: 'When the mind is defiled, beings are defiled; when the mind is pure, beings are pure.'"

"Caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ" refers to a wandering picture (a show-picture). There are Brahmin heretics called Saṅkhā; they make a picture-box and have various successes and failures depicted there according to the heavenly and miserable realms, and they wander about holding that picture, showing that "by doing this action, one receives this; by doing that, one receives that." "Citteneve cittitaṃ" means it is called "thought out by the mind" because it was created by the artist after thinking it out with his mind. "Cittaññeva cittataraṃ" means the mind that seeks the means to paint that picture is even more intricate than the picture itself. "Animals are diversified by the mind" means they are made diverse only by the kamma-consciousness. Regarding that kamma-consciousness, it is not that these quails, partridges, and so forth strive thinking, "We shall have such diverse colors." Rather, kamma leads them to the womb (yoni), and their mental state (individuality) is rooted in that womb. Beings who have entered a womb have minds (individualities) similar to those of that particular womb. Thus, it should be understood that the diversity is accomplished by the womb, and the womb is accomplished by kamma.
300:
Moreover, this mind should be understood as even more variegated than the minds of animals, because of the variegated nature of conascent (sahajāta) states, planes (bhūmi), bases (vatthu), doors (dvāra), and objects (ārammaṇa), and because it produces many kinds of minds based on the diversity of kamma, gender (liṅga), perception (saññā), and designation (vohāra).

A dyer (or a painter) creates forms on cloth with dye. If he is unskilled, he creates an unpleasant form; if he is skilled, he creates a pleasant and beautiful form. In the same way, a worldling (puthujjana), through an unwholesome mind or a wholesome mind dissociated from knowledge, produces an ugly individual existence (attabhāva) devoid of the perfection of the eyes (cakkhusampadā) and so on. However, through a wholesome mind associated with knowledge, he produces a very beautiful individual existence endowed with the perfection of the eyes and so on. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Vāsijaṭasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, the Vāsijaṭa Sutta, the Buddha taught two similes—the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) and the bright side (sukkapakkha)—starting with "Monks, suppose there were a hen's eggs..." Among these two, the dark side simile does not complete the meaning, while only the other, the bright side simile, completes the meaning. The meaning of the bright side simile should be understood thus: "Seyyathā" is a particle meaning "just as" (simile); "api" is a particle meaning "perhaps" or "suppose" (conjecture). Through both words, he shows, "Monks, it might be thus." In the phrase "eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen," although there may be fewer or more eggs than the stated number, it is said this way for the sake of linguistic smoothness. Such an expression is very smooth in common usage. "Tānassu" means "tāni assu" (those eggs might be). "Properly sat upon by the hen" means they are well sat upon by that mother hen spreading her wings over those eggs. "Properly warmed" means they are well warmed and heated all around by letting them receive heat from time to time. "Properly seasoned" means they are well prepared all around from time to time, meaning they are made to take on the scent of the hen.

Even if that hen, while performing these three actions without negligence, does not have the wish, "May it be so," nevertheless, those chicks are capable of safely breaking the eggshell and emerging according to the stated method. This is because, as those eggs are protected by the hen through these three ways, they do not rot. The moisture within those eggs also reaches a state of drying up. The eggshell becomes thin. The tips of the claws and the tips of the beaks also become hard. The chicks themselves reach maturity. Because the eggshell is thin, the light from outside becomes visible inside the shell. Therefore, from that light outside...
301:
Those eggs do not rot; the sticky moisture of those eggs reaches a state of drying up; the eggshell is thin; the tips of the claws and the tips of the beaks are firm and hard; the chicks themselves reach maturity. Because the eggshell is thin, the light from outside is clear within. Therefore, thinking, "For a long time indeed we have slept in a narrow place with our hands and feet curled; now this light from outside is visible; now our happy dwelling will be in this place," they desire to go out and kick the eggshell with their feet and stretch their necks. By doing so, that eggshell breaks into two. Then, those chicks, flapping their wings and chirping appropriately for that moment, emerge completely. Having emerged, they wander about, beautifying the vicinity of the village.

"Evam-eva kho" (Even so) is the application of the simile. It should be understood by comparing it with the following meaning: Just as the hen performs the three actions on the eggs, so should the time when this monk is devoted to meditation (bhāvanānuyoga) be understood. Just as the eggs do not rot because the hen fulfills the three actions, so should the non-decline of insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) be understood because the monk devoted to meditation fulfills the three contemplations (anupassanā). Just as the moisture dries up because the hen performs the three actions, so should the drying up of the moisture of attachment (nikanti-taṇhā) that follows the three realms of existence be understood because the monk fulfills the three contemplations. Just as the eggshells become thin, so should the thinning of the monk's eggshell of ignorance (avijjā) be understood. Just as the tips of the chicks' claws and beaks become firm and hard, so should the sharpness of the monk's insight knowledge be understood—its keenness due to concentration (samādhi), its steadiness due to mindfulness (sati), its clarity due to faith (saddhā), and its courage due to energy (viriya). Just as the time of the chicks' maturity, so should the time of the maturation of the monk's insight knowledge, the time of its development, and the time of "taking the conception" of the Path knowledge be understood. Just as the time when the chicks break the eggshell with the tips of their claws or beaks, flap their wings, and emerge safely, so should the time be understood when this monk, while wandering about having "taken the conception" of insight knowledge, obtains suitable climate (utu-sappāya), suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), a suitable person (puggala-sappāya), or the suitable hearing of the Dhamma (dhammassavana-sappāya), and while developing insight even while sitting in a single session, breaks the eggshell of ignorance with the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) attained in due order, flaps the wings of direct knowledge (abhiññā), and safely reaches the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). Just as the mother hen, knowing the maturity of the chicks, also breaks the eggshell, even so, the Blessed One, knowing the maturation of the knowledge of such a monk—
302:
“Cut off your own affection, as one plucks an autumn lotus with the hand. Cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.” (Dhp 285) — By this and other such means, the Blessed One emitted a radiance and struck the shell of ignorance with this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, that monk broke the shell of ignorance and attained Arahantship. From then on, just as those young chicks wander about beautifying the village grounds, so too this great Arahant wandered about beautifying the monastery (saṅghārāma), dwelling in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object.

Palagaṇḍa refers to a carpenter. He is called palagaṇḍa because he holds a plumb line (olambaka) and removes the knots of the wood. Vāsijaṭa refers to the place where the handle of the adze is held by the hand. “Today, so many of my taints (āsavas) are exhausted” means that for one who has gone forth, the taints are constantly exhausted through learning, inquiry, wise reflection, and the practice of duties. However, as they are being exhausted, the knowledge does not arise that “this much was exhausted today, that much yesterday.” By this simile, the benefits of insight (vipassanā) are illustrated. Hemantikena means by the winter season. Paṭippassambhanti means they decline from their stable state.

“Evameva kho” (In the same way): In this context, the Dispensation (sāsana) should be seen as the great ocean. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be seen as a boat. Dwelling with teachers and preceptors during the period before completing five years is like the boat remaining in the great ocean for a long time. The weakening of the fetters (saṃyojana) through learning, inquiry, and so forth is like the rotting of the boat's bindings due to the ocean water. Dwelling in the forest after becoming independent (nissayamuttaka) and taking up a meditation subject is like the time the boat is hauled onto dry land. The drying up of the moisture of craving by the power of insight-knowledge is like the drying by the sun and wind during the day. The moistening of the mind with joy and gladness (pītipāmojja) arising based on the meditation subject is like the moistening by dew at night. The extreme weakening of the fetters through insight-knowledge, joy, and gladness after obtaining suitable weather and other conditions is like the weakening and rotting of the bindings due to the sun, wind, and dew day and night. The knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa) is like a great cloud at the start of the rainy season. Just as the boat's bindings rot away due to the rainwater...
303: For a monk who has begun insight (āraddhavipassaka) and is developing insight by way of the sevenfold group of form (rūpasattaka) and so on, when the meditation subject becomes clear and distinct as it reaches the right path, one day, having obtained suitable weather and so forth, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship while sitting in a single cross-legged posture should be noted (like the falling away of the bindings of a rotting boat). Just as a boat whose rattan bindings are rotting remains for a short time, the Arahant whose fetters are destroyed remains until the end of his life-span while assisting the great multitude. Just as a rotting boat gradually breaks up and reaches a state where it can no longer be designated, the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, upon the breakup of the karmically acquired aggregates (upādinna-kkhandha), attains Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and reaches a state where no designation or physical form remains. By this analogy, the weakness of the fetters is shown. The ninth sutta is finished. ## 10. Aniccasaññāsutta-vaṇṇanā In the tenth sutta, "aniccasaññā" (perception of impermanence) is the perception that arises in one who develops [the thought] "impermanent, impermanent." "Pariyādiyati" means it exhausts or consumes. "Sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ" refers to the ninefold conceit "I am." "Mūlasantānakāni" means roots that stand spread out in a continuous line. The perception of impermanence is like a great plough; the defilements are like small and very small roots. Just as a farmer plowing with a plough cuts and uproots those roots, so too the yogi, developing the perception of impermanence, cuts and uproots the defilements with the knowledge of the perception of impermanence. This is the comparison with the analogy here. "Odhunāti" means he shakes down. "Niddhunāti" means he shakes out. "Nicchoṭeti" means he shakes off and discards. In this analogy also, the defilements are like pubbā grass; the knowledge of the perception of impermanence is like reaping and shaking off. The analogy should be compared with this meaning. "Vaṇṭacchinnāya" means when it is cut at the stalk by a sharp arrow. "Tadanvayāni bhavanti" means they follow after that bunch of mangoes; when that bunch falls, the mangoes fall to the ground. Here too, the defilements are like the bunch of mangoes; the perception of impermanence is like the sharp arrow. Just as all the mangoes fall to the ground from a bunch cut by an arrow, so too, when ignorance (avijjā), which is the root of the defilements, is cut by the knowledge of the perception of impermanence, all defilements reach utter destruction. This is the comparison with the analogy. "Kūṭaṅgamā" means they go to the roof peak. "Kūṭaninnā" means they incline toward the roof peak by way of entering it. "Kūṭasamosaraṇā" means they stand assembled at the roof peak. Here too, the perception of impermanence is like the roof peak; the wholesome states belonging to the four planes are like the rafters. How so?...
304:
Just as the peak is the highest among all rafters, so too, among all wholesome states, the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) is the highest. If it is asked, 'Is not the perception of impermanence mundane? Let it be the highest among mundane wholesome states, but how is it the highest among supramundane states?', it should be understood that it is the highest because it is the cause for the attainment of those supramundane states. In this way, the comparison between the simile and the thing signified should be understood in all the similes. Herein, the function of the perception of impermanence is shown by the first three similes, and its power is shown by the subsequent similes. The tenth sutta is finished.

In the tenth sutta, 'approached' (upasaṅkami) means that after seeing other monks request the meditation subject on the five aggregates, and by striving and exerting themselves, reach Arahantship and declare their attainment in the presence of the Teacher, [Ānanda] thought: 'I too will request the meditation subject on the five aggregates, and by striving and exerting myself, I will declare Arahantship when I reach it,' and so he approached. "Sought" (pariyiesita) refers to an object that was sought, whether it was obtained or not. "Pondered by the mind" (anuvicaritaṃ manasā) refers to an object that has been repeatedly thought about with the mind. In the world, there are objects that are obtained after being sought, objects that are not obtained despite being sought, objects that are obtained without being sought, and objects that are not obtained and not sought. Among these four, an object obtained after being sought is called "patta." An object not obtained after being sought is called "pariyiesita." Both an object obtained without being sought and an object not obtained without being sought are called "manasānuvicarita." Alternatively, both an object obtained after being sought and an object obtained without being sought are called "patta" in the sense of being attained; only an object not obtained after being sought is called "pariyiesita"; and an object not obtained without being sought is called "manasānuvicarita." Or, all of these are simply "manasā anuvicarita" because they are all repeatedly pondered by the mind.
