## 5. Commentary on Natthidinna Sutta

In the words beginning with "natthi dinnaṃ," "natthi dinnaṃ" is said with reference to the absence of fruit from giving gifts. A great sacrifice (mahādāna) is called "yiṭṭha." The term "huta" refers to hospitality shown to guests. They reject both "yiṭṭha" and "huta" by intending that they have no fruit. "Sukata-dukkata" means wholesome and unwholesome actions (kamma). "Phalaṃ vipāko" means that which is called fruit (phala) or ripening (vipāka); they say that such fruit does not exist. "Natthi ayaṃ loko" means that for one established in the next world, this world does not exist. "Natthi paro loko" means that even for one established in this world, the next world does not exist; they show that all beings are annihilated (ucchijjati) right in those respective existences. "Natthi mātā natthi pitā" is said because of the absence of fruit from right or wrong conduct toward parents. "Natthi sattā opapātikā" means they say there are no beings who are reborn after passing away. "Natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā" means they say there are no recluses or brahmins in the world who have practiced rightly.

"Cātumahābhūtiko" means a body composed of the four great elements. "Pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ" means the internal earth element returns to the external earth element. "Anupeti" means to approach or go towards. "Anupagacchati" is a synonym for that same word "anupeti"; it also has the meaning "anugacchati" (to follow). By both terms, they show the process of approaching. The same method applies to the liquid element (āpo) and so forth. "Indriyāni" refers to the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth. "Saṅkamanti" means they pass into space. "Āsandipañcamā" refers to the five things including the bier; it means the bier itself and the four men standing and holding the four legs of the bier. "Yāva āḷāhanā" means up to the cemetery. "Padāni" refers to words (terms) expressing virtues and vices, such as "This person was virtuous in this way, this person was immoral in that way." Alternatively, "padāni" here refers to the body itself. "Kāpotakāni" means having the color of a dove, meaning the color of a pigeon's wing. "Bhassantā" means ending in ashes. Alternatively, this very word is the original Pali. "Āhutiyo" means whatever gifts are given, such as hospitality and so forth; the meaning is that all such giving ends only in ashes and does not go further to become a giver of fruit. "Dattupaññattaṃ" means that which is laid down by fools (dattu). The intended meaning is: this giving is laid down by fools who lack wisdom, not by the wise. They show that fools give and the wise receive.
312:
## 6. Commentary on the Karoto Sutta

"Karoto" refers to one who performs an action personally with one's own hand. "Kārayato" refers to one who causes an action to be performed by command. "Chindato" refers to one who cuts off the hands, feet, ears, etc., of others. "Chedāpayato" refers to one who causes others to cut them off. "Pacato" refers to one who oppresses others with punishments. "Pacāpayato" refers to one who causes others who follow one's words to oppress with punishments and so on. "Socato socāpayato" refers to both one who personally causes grief and one who causes others to cause grief through acts such as stealing the property of others. "Kilamato kilamāpayato" refers to both one who personally causes weariness and one who causes others to cause weariness through acts such as cutting off food, binding, or imprisonment. "Phandato phandāpayato" refers to both one who personally trembles through the effort of oppressing others when causing them to tremble, and one who causes others to tremble. "Pāṇamatipātayato" refers to both one who personally kills living beings and one who causes them to be killed. Thus, in all instances, the meaning should be understood through the power of doing and causing to do.

"Sandhiṃ" refers to the junction of house walls (breaking in). "Nillopaṃ" refers to robbery (great plundering). "Ekāgārikaṃ" refers to plundering by surrounding only a single house. "Paripanthe tiṭṭhato" refers to one who waits on the path to rob whoever comes. "Karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ" means that even for one who acts with the perception "I will do all kinds of evil without limit," no evil is done; there is no such thing as evil. It is shown that beings merely have the perception "We will do evil." "Khurapariyantena" refers to a wheel-like weapon with an edge as sharp as a razor. "Ekamaṃsakhalaṃ" means a single heap of flesh. "Puñjaṃ" is just a synonym for that heap of flesh. "Tatonidānaṃ" means having the making of that single heap of flesh as the cause.

"Dakkhiṇaṃ" refers to the people living on the south bank of the Ganges who are harsh and cruel; "killing," etc., is stated in reference to them. "Uttaraṃ" refers to the people living on the north bank of the Ganges who have faith and are devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; "giving," etc., is stated in reference to them. In that context of giving, "yajanto" refers to one who performs a great sacrifice. "Damena" refers to the restraint of the senses and the observance of the Uposatha. "Saṃyamena" refers to restraint through virtue (sīla). "Saccavajjena" refers to speaking truthful words. "Āgamo" means coming or arising. In every way, they reject the efficacy of both evil and merit.
313:
## 7. Commentary on the Hetu Sutta

In the phrase "Natthi hetu natthi paccayo," the word "paccayo" is just a synonym for "hetu." By both terms, they reject the causes of defilement (saṃkilesapaccaya) such as bodily misconduct, and the causes of purification (visuddhipaccaya) such as bodily good conduct, even though these causes clearly exist. "Natthi balaṃ" means they reject that strength (bala) by which these beings, established in their own strength, attain the state of a deity, a Māra, a Brahmā, the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi), the enlightenment of a private Buddha (paccekabodhi), and omniscience (sabbaññuta). "Natthi vīriyaṃ" and all such terms are just synonyms for one another. However, they are taken separately in the sense of rejecting statements like "This was attained by our energy," "This was attained by human strength," or "This was attained by human endeavor."

By the term "sabbe sattā," they include all beings without exception, such as camels, oxen, donkeys, and horses. By the term "sabbe pāṇā," they speak in terms of one-sensed beings, two-sensed beings, and so on. The term "sabbe bhūtā" is said in reference to beings born from egg-shells and wombs. The term "sabbe jīvā" is said in reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so on. Because these plants have the nature of growing, they have the perception that they possess life (jīva). "Avasā abalā avīriyā" means that those beings, breathing things, etc., have no power, strength, or energy of their own. In the term "niyatisangati-bhāva-pariṇatā," "niyati" is destiny (fixedness). "Sangati" is the meeting of the six classes of birth (abhijāti) in various existences. "Bhāva" is just nature (sabhāva). Thus, they are transformed and reach various states through destiny, coincidence, and nature. They show that whatever is to happen to someone happens exactly so. What is not to happen does not happen. "Chasvevābhijātīsu" means they experience pleasure and pain while established only in the six classes of birth; they show that there is no other ground for experiencing pleasure and pain.

## 8-10. Commentary on the Mahādiṭṭhi Sutta, etc.

213-215. "Akaṭā" means things that are not made. "Akaṭavidhā" means things that are not created; it means they are not even caused to be done by someone saying "Do it like this." "Animmitā" means not created even by psychic power. "Animmātā" means not caused to be created. There is also a reading "animmitabbā," meaning they cannot be created. "Vañjhā" means barren; like barren animals or barren palm trees, they are fruitless and do not produce anything. Because they stand like mountain peaks, they are called "kūṭaṭṭhā." Because they stand firmly like gate-posts, they are called "esikaṭṭhāyiဋ္ဌိတာ"; it means they stand as a firmly planted gate-post stands motionless. "Na iñjanti" means like a gate-post...
314:
They do not shake because they stand unshakable like a gatepost. They do not undergo change because they do not abandon their original nature. They do not oppress or harm one another. 'Nālaṃ' means being incapable. The earth element itself or a collection of earth is called the earth-body (pathavīkāya). Regarding the seven bodies, just as a weapon enters through the gaps in a heap of mung beans and the like, so too does a weapon pass through the gaps and openings between the seven bodies. In that case, the thought 'I shall deprive this person of life' is merely a perception. (This means there is no killing because the body cannot be destroyed.)

They present their own baseless views, stating that there are 1,400,000 main birth-origins (yoni) of the noble type, another 100,000, another 6,600, and 500 kinds of kamma. The same method applies to the five kammas and three kammas. Some teachers consider the five kammas in terms of the five sense faculties (indriya), and the three kammas in terms of bodily, verbal, and mental action. In the view of 'a kamma and a half-kamma,' coarse bodily and verbal actions are considered full kammas, while subtle mental action is considered a half-kamma. They say there are sixty-two paths of practice (paṭipadā). Although there are sixty-four intermediate aeons (antarakappa) in one aeon, this teacher (Makkhali Gosāla) says there are sixty-two intermediate aeons because he is unaware of the other two.

The six classes (abhijāti) are: the black class (kaṇhā), the blue class (nīlā), the red class (lohitā), the yellow class (haliddā), the white class (sukkā), and the purest white class (paramasukkā). Among these six, sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, fowlers, hunters, deer-hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, jailers, and others who perform cruel deeds are called the black class (kaṇhābhijāti). Monks are called the blue class (nīlābhijāti). It is said that these monks use the four requisites by inserting things like thorns into them. The Pali 'Monks have a thorn-like livelihood' is indeed the doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla. Alternatively, some ascetics outside the dispensation who practice like thorns are called the blue class. Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single garment are called the red class (lohitābhijāti). These are said to be purer than the previous two. White-clothed laypeople and disciples of the Acelakas are called the yellow class (haliddābhijāti). In this way, they make their own supporters even greater than the Nigaṇṭhas. Ājīvaka monks and nuns are called the white class (sukkābhijāti). They are said to be purer than the previous four. Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla are called the purest white class (paramasukkābhijāti). They are said to be the purest of all. The eight stages of man (purisabhūmi) are: mandabhūmi, ḍaharabhūmi, vīmaṃsābhūmi, ujugatabhūmi, sekhabhūmi, samaṇabhūmi, jinabhūmi...
315:
Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla are said to be the purest white class (paramasukkābhijāti). They are especially purer than all others.

The eight stages of man (aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo) are said to be: mandabhūmi, khiḍḍābhūmi, vīmaṃsakabhūmi, ujugatabhūmi, sekhabhūmi, samaṇabhūmi, jānanabhūmi, and pannabhūmi. Among these eight, from the day of birth for seven days, because they have emerged from the narrow mother's womb, infants are extremely confused; this is called mandabhūmi. Those who come from the states of misery (duggati) constantly weep and wail, remembering that realm; those who come from the states of happiness (sugati) laugh, remembering that realm; this is called khiḍḍābhūmi. The period when they hold the hands, feet, couch, or stool of their parents and place their feet on the ground is called vīmaṃsakabhūmi. The period when they are able to walk by themselves is called ujugatabhūmi. The period when they learn arts and sciences is called sekhabhūmi. The period when they leave home and go forth as monks is called samaṇabhūmi. The period when they attend upon a teacher and know what is the practice and what is not is called jānanabhūmi. Saying 'The monk is aged and no longer speaks anything,' such a monk with few gains is called pannabhūmi.

There are 4,900 Ājīvakas, 4,900 Wanderers (Paribbājakas), 4,900 Naga-abodes, 2,000 faculties (indriya), and 3,000 hells. Rajodhātu refers to places covered with dust and dirt, such as the backs of the hands and feet. The seven types of sentient wombs (saññīgabbha) refer to camels, cattle, donkeys, goats, deer, wild animals, and buffaloes. The seven types of insentient wombs (asaññīgabbha) refer to hill paddy, crops, wheat, mung beans, millet, barley, and rice. Nigaṇṭhigabbha refers to those born from knots or joints, such as sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and the like. Although there are many gods, Makkhali says there are only seven types. Although humans are infinite, he says there are only seven types. Although demons (pisāca) are very many, he says there are only seven types. The great lakes (sarā) refer to the seven great lakes: Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhappapāta, Chaddanta, Mucalinda, and Kuṇāla.

Pavuṭā means knots or protuberances. Papātā means great precipices. Papātasatāni means hundreds of small precipices. Supinā means great dreams. Supinasatāni means hundreds of small dreams. Mahākappino refers to the number of great aeons (mahākappa). Among these seven great lakes, the time it takes for the water in one great lake to be exhausted by taking one drop of water with the tip of a blade of samana grass once every hundred years is called one great aeon (mahākappa).
316:
Every hundred years, if one takes a drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, and when that lake is thus emptied of water, it is called one Great Aeon (Mahākappa). After passing through eight million four hundred thousand such Great Aeons, both fools and the wise will make an end of suffering—this is the view of Makkhali. It means that even the wise cannot attain purity in the interval, and the fool cannot go beyond that time.

'By virtue' means by the virtue of an ascetic (acelaka) or any other virtue. 'By practice' means by such a practice. 'By austerity' means by the practice of penance (tapokamma). 'Makes the unripe ripe' means one who says 'I am wise' and tries to attain purity in the interval. 'Having reached the ripe, makes it vanish' means one who says 'I am a fool' and goes beyond the designated time. It is shown that neither of these—making the unripe ripe or making the ripe vanish—is possible. 'Like a measured doṇa' means as if measured by a doṇa measure. 'Happiness and suffering' refers to pleasure and pain. 'Finite' means limited by the aforementioned time. 'There is no decrease or increase' means there is no waning or waxing. The saṃsāra of the wise does not decrease, and the saṃsāra of the fool does not increase. 'Exaltation and depression' (ukkansāvakaṃsa) are synonyms for increase and decrease.

Now, to illustrate this meaning with a simile, he said 'Just as, for instance' (seyyathāpi nāma), etc. There, 'a ball of thread' (suttaguḷa) means a ball made by winding thread. 'It runs along only as it unwinds' means a ball of thread thrown while standing on a mountain or a treetop goes only as far as the length of the thread as it unwinds, and when the thread is exhausted, it stops right there. In the same way, fools and the wise experience the pleasure and pain that unwind by the power of time, and they transcend saṃsāra after the aforementioned time.

## 11-18. Commentary on the Antavā Sutta, etc.

216-223. 'The world is finite' is a view (diṭṭhi) that arises either by grasping or by reasoning that the world is the sign of a kasina developed on one side. 'The world is infinite' is a view that arises either by grasping or by reasoning that the world is the sign of an immeasurable kasina developed all around. 'That soul is that body' is a view that arises that the soul (jīva) and the body (sarīra) are one and the same. The remaining words are clear in all places. These are the eighteen expositions (veyyākaraṇa) according to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), forming one sequence (gamana).
317:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Gamana-vaggas, etc.

224-301. The second Gamana-peyyāla is taught by way of suffering (dukkha). In that second sequence also, there are only eighteen discourses that have the characteristic of an exposition (veyyākaraṇa). Following those eighteen, eight discourses having the characteristic of an exposition such as 'The self is material' (rūpī attā hoti) are taught. Together with those eight, that second sequence is called the second repetition (peyyāla).

Among those eight discourses, 'material' (rūpī) is the view that grasps only the object (ārammaṇa), such as a kasina, as 'the self'. 'Immaterial' (arūpī) is the view that grasps jhāna as 'the self'. 'Both material and immaterial' is the view that grasps both the object and the jhāna as 'the self'. 'Neither material nor immaterial' is the view grasped by mere reasoning (takka). 'Exclusively happy' (ekantasukhī) is the view that arises for those who have attained (lābhī), those who reason (takkī), and those who remember past lives (jātissara). For those who have attained jhāna, when they reflect on a past existence that was purely happy, such a view arises. For the reasoner, it arises from the thought: 'Just as I am exclusively happy now, so I will be in the future.' For the one who remembers past lives, it arises when seeing a happy state in seven or eight past lives. In the case of 'exclusively suffering' (ekantadukkhī), etc., the same method applies.

The third repetition (peyyāla) is taught by way of impermanence (anicca) and suffering (dukkha) through those same twenty-six discourses. The fourth repetition is taught by way of the three rounds (tiparivaṭṭa).

## The Commentary on the Diṭṭhi Saṃyutta is finished.

## 4. Okkanta Saṃyutta

## 1-10. Commentary on the Cakkhu Sutta, etc.

302-311. In the Okkanta Saṃyutta, 'is resolved' (adhimuccati) means obtaining the resolution of faith (saddhādhimokkha). 'Entered the path of assurance' (okkanto sammattaniyāmaṃ) means having entered the Noble Path (ariyamagga). By the words 'incapable of passing away during that time', he shows that once the Path has arisen, there is no obstacle to the Fruit (phala). Indeed, when the Path has arisen, there is nothing that can cause an obstacle to the Fruit. Therefore, he said: 'If this person were practicing for the realization of the Fruit of Stream-entry, and it were the time for the world-cycle to burn up, the world-cycle would not burn up as long as this person has not realized the Fruit of Stream-entry; this person is called one who stays for the aeon (ṭhitakappī).' 'They endure reflection to a certain extent' (mattaso nijjhānaṃ khamanti) means they endure observation according to measure. The remaining words are clear in all the discourses.

## The Commentary on the Okkanta Saṃyutta is finished.
318:
## 5. Commentary on the Uppādasamyutta
312–321. In the Uppādasamyutta, everything is clear.

## The Commentary on the Uppādasamyutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Kilesasamyutta
322–331. In the Kilesasamyutta, regarding the statement "this desire and lust (chandarāga) is a corruption (upakkilesa) of the mind," which mind is meant? It refers to the mind of the four planes (catubhūmaka-citta). Let alone the fact that corruption can afflict the mind of the three planes; how can there be corruption for the supramundane mind (lokuttara-citta)? It is called a corruption because it prevents its arising. That desire and lust should be understood as a corruption because it does not allow the supramundane mind to arise. "Nekkhammaninnaṃ" means inclining towards the nine supramundane states. "Cittaṃ" refers to the mind of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). "Abhiññā sacchika-raṇīyesu dhammesu" occurs in the six higher knowledges (dhammas associated with the noble path) that are to be directly known and realized through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). Alternatively, when one wishes to take a single dhamma among the nine supramundane states, namely Nibbāna, it should be taken as "nekkhamma." All the remaining Pali text is clear in meaning.

## The Commentary on the Kilesasamyutta is finished.

## 7. Sāriputtasamyutta

## 1–9. Commentary on the Vivekajasutta, etc.
332–340. In the first discourse of the Sāriputtasamyutta, "it does not occur like this" means that because I-making (ahaṅkāra) and mine-making (mamaṅkāra) have been abandoned, there is no such reflection as "I will enter the first jhāna, I have entered it, or I have emerged from the jhāna." The same method should be understood for the second discourse and so on.

## 10. Commentary on the Sucimukhīsutta
In the tenth discourse, "Sucimukhī" is the name of a female wanderer (paribbājikā). "Upasaṅkami" means that upon seeing the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, who was very handsome, pleasant to look at, golden-hued, and inspiring in every way, she approached him thinking, "I will tease this monk." Then, when the Thera rejected those words...
319:
Thinking, "Now I will find fault with this monk," she asked, "Monk, if that is so, do you eat facing upwards (ubbhāmukha)?" "Disāmukha" means eating while facing the four cardinal directions and looking towards them. "Vidisāmukha" means eating while looking towards the four intermediate directions.

"Vatthuvijjā-tiracchānavijjā" refers to the low art (tiracchānavijjā) known as the science of building sites. The science of building sites (vatthuvijjā) is the means of knowing the proper time for the success of crops in fields such as gourds, pumpkins, radishes, and so on. "Micchājီvena jīvikaṃ kappenti" means they make a living by this wrong livelihood called the science of building sites and low arts; it means they live by consuming the requisites offered by people who are inspired by their making those fields productive. "Adhomukha" (facing downwards) means eating by way of looking at the fields and grounds. In this way, the application should be understood in all instances.

Furthermore, in this context, "nakkhattavijjā" (astrology) is the art of knowing, "Today this constellation will travel in conjunction with that constellation; such and such a task should be performed with this constellation." "Dūteyya" (messenger-work) is the act of a messenger, taking the news of various people and going to various places. "Pahiṇagamana" (running errands) means going from one family to another within the same village with a message. "Aṅgavijjā" (physiognomy) is the art of knowing the perfection of limbs by way of the marks of women and men, thinking, "By this perfection of limbs, such and such a benefit will be obtained." "Vidisāmukha" means that because the art of physiognomy proceeds by taking various parts of the body as its object, it is said to proceed in the intermediate directions (vidisā); therefore, those who make a living and eat by that art are said to eat facing the intermediate directions.

"Evamārocesi" means that while saying "Monks practice in accordance with the Dhamma," etc., she spoke of the virtue of the Dispensation (Sāsana) that leads out of suffering. Having heard the words of that female wanderer, about five hundred families entered the Dispensation.

## The Commentary on the Sāriputtasamyutta is finished.

## 8. Nāgasamyutta

## 1. Commentary on the Suddhikasutta
In the Nāgasamyutta, "aṇḍaja" refers to those born from an egg. "Jalābuja" refers to those born from a womb. "Saṃsedaja" refers to those born from moisture. "Opapātika" refers to those...
320:
Spontaneously born (opapātika) nāgas arise as if they have fallen from some place above. This sutta was spoken because a specific occasion arose. Among the monks, a discussion occurred: "How many types of nāga births are there?" Then, the Blessed One, wishing to reveal the types of nāga births for the sake of uplifting those who are trainable, spoke this sutta.

## 2-50. Commentary on the Paṇītatara Sutta, etc.
343-391. In the second sutta and others, "vossaṭṭhakāyā" means having bodies that are relinquished without regard for the oppression of snake charmers. "Dvayakārino" means those who habitually perform two types of deeds: wholesome and unwholesome. "Sacajja mayaṃ" means "If we today..." "Sahabyataṃ upapajjati" means attaining companionship (rebirth in the nāga realm). For such a person, unwholesome karma is the condition for rebirth, while wholesome karma is the condition for the prosperity and happiness that arise.

"Annaṃ" refers to food and edibles. "Pānaṃ" refers to any kind of drink. "Vatthaṃ" refers to clothing and robes. "Yānaṃ" refers to means of travel such as umbrellas and sandals. "Mālaṃ" refers to flowers such as jasmine. "Gandhaṃ" refers to scents such as sandalwood. "Vilepanaṃ" refers to ointments for the skin. "Seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ" means giving bedding such as couches and benches, dwellings such as single-storied monasteries, and lighting requisites such as wicks and oil. Wishing for the long life, beauty, and abundant happiness of those nāgas, they give these ten types of gifts and are reborn in that nāga realm to enjoy that prosperity. The remaining terms are clear in all the suttas.

## The Commentary on the Nāga Saṃyutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Supaṇṇa Saṃyutta
392-437. In the Supaṇṇa Saṃyutta, garuḷas are called "supaṇṇa" (well-winged) because of the beauty and intricacy of their wings. In this sutta as well, the first sutta was spoken according to the previous method based on the occasion. "Haranti" means they snatch (seize) from the ocean. In snatching, those garuḷas can only snatch nāgas who are inferior to them or equal to them; they are not able to snatch those who are superior to themselves.

In truth, there are seven types of superior nāgas who cannot be snatched. They are: the Kambalassatara nāgas, the Dhataraṭṭha nāgas, the nāgas dwelling in the seven Sīdantara oceans, the earth-dwelling nāgas, the mountain-dwelling nāgas, and the mansion-dwelling nāgas. Among those nāgas, compared to the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and others, the womb-born (jalābuja) and others are...
321:
...superior, and they cannot be snatched by those garuḷas. The Kambalassatara nāgas are nāga generals; therefore, wherever they are seen, no garuḷa whatsoever can snatch them. The Dhataraṭṭha nāgas are nāga kings; they too cannot be snatched by any garuḷa. As for the nāgas who dwell within the seven Sīdantara great oceans, because it is impossible to cause them any vibration, no garuḷa can snatch them. For the earth-dwelling nāgas and others, there is the opportunity for hiding; therefore, they too cannot be snatched. However, as for the nāgas who dwell on the surface of the waves of the great ocean, a garuḷa who is either equal to them or superior can snatch them. The rest is exactly as explained in the Nāga Saṃyutta.

## The Commentary on the Supaṇṇa Saṃyutta is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Gandhabbakāya Saṃyutta
438-549. In the Gandhabbakāya Saṃyutta, "mūlagandhe adhivatthā" refers to deities who arise depending on the scent of a tree's roots. That entire tree is useful to those deities. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Gandhagandhe" refers to the collective scent of various scents such as roots. If a tree has scent in all its parts such as roots, it is called "gandha" here. They reside in that scent. Here, all parts such as roots are useful to those deities. "That person is a giver of root-scents" means being a giver of root-scents such as kāḷānusāri. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all terms. In this way, they make a resolution after giving a gift that is either similar or dissimilar to the result they will receive. To show that gift, the ten types of gifts are spoken of, starting with "He gives food." The remaining terms are clear in all the suttas.

## The Commentary on the Gandhabbakāya Saṃyutta is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Valāhaka Saṃyutta
550-606. In the Valāhaka Saṃyutta, "valāhaka-kāyikā" refers to sky-faring deities born in the group of deities named Valāhaka. "Sīta-valāhaka" are the Valāhaka deities who cause cold. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Cetopaṇidhimanvāya" means based on the resolution of the mind. "Cold occurs" means the cold that occurs in the rainy season or winter is merely ordinary cold caused by the season. However, the cold that occurs during extreme cold or the cold that occurs in the summer is called cold caused by the power and majesty of the deities. "Heat occurs" means the heat that occurs in the summer is merely ordinary heat caused by the season. However, the heat that occurs during extreme heat or the heat that occurs in the winter is called heat caused by the majesty of the deities. "A cloud occurs" means the appearance of cloud layers and masses that cover like a large pavilion. Thus, the clouds that occur during the Valāhaka winds, the rainy season, and the winter season are merely ordinary clouds caused by the season. However, during the time of rising clouds, they cover the moon and sun for seven days or seven months, creating dense layers of clouds.
322:
In the winter season, coldness occurs; that coldness is simply caused by the season (utu). However, extreme coldness even during the cold season, or coldness that arises in the summer, is called coldness produced by the power of the deities (devatānubhāva). 'Heat occurs' means the heat that occurs in the summer, which is just the normal heat caused by the season. However, extreme heat even during the hot season, or heat that arises in the winter, is called heat produced by the power of the deities. 'Clouds occur' means the formation of a canopy of clouds. Here too, the clouds that arise in the rainy season and the sisira (cool) season are just normal clouds caused by the season. However, extreme cloudiness even when it is cloudy, covering the moon and sun for as long as seven times seven days (49 days) and creating absolute darkness, or clouds that arise in the months of Citta and Vesākha, are called clouds produced by the power of the deities. 'Wind blows' means the normal wind that blows from the north, south, etc., in various seasons, which is simply caused by the season. However, the extremely violent wind that can split tree trunks and the like, and winds that blow out of season, are called winds produced by the power of the deities. 'It rains' means the rain that falls throughout the four months of the rainy season, which is simply caused by the season. However, excessive rain even during the rainy season, and rain that falls in the months of Citta and Vesākha, is called rain produced by the power of the deities.

In this regard, there is this story—It is said that a certain Vassa-valāhaka devaputta (rain-cloud deity) went to an Arahant Elder residing at Talakūṭaka, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you?" "Venerable sir, I am a Vassa-valāhaka devaputta," he replied. "Is it true that it rains according to your will (mind)?" the Elder asked. "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "We wish to see it," the Elder said. "Venerable sir, you will get wet," he replied. "Neither the head of a cloud nor thunder is apparent yet; how shall we get wet?" the Elder said. "Venerable sir, it rains by my mind; please enter the leaf-roofed hut (paṇṇasālā)," he replied. "Very well, son of the devas," the Elder said, and after washing his feet, he entered the hut. As soon as the Elder entered the hut, the son of the devas sang a song and raised his hand. Immediately, a single massive cloud formed over an area of three yojanas all around. The Elder entered the hut while being half-drenched. Furthermore, rain falls due to eight causes: the power of the nāgas, the power of the supaṇṇas (garudas), the power of the deities, the act of truth (saccakiriyā), the change of seasons (utu), the interference of Māra, the power of psychic potency (iddhi), and the rain of world-destruction (vināsamegha).

## The Commentary on the Valāhaka Saṃyutta is finished.

## 12. Vacchagottasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā

607-661. In the Vacchagotta Saṃyutta, 'aññāṇā' means by way of ignorance (aññāṇa—the delusion that covers the Four Noble Truths). In this way, the meaning in all terms should be understood by the power of the instrumental case (karaṇa). All these terms—aññāṇa (ignorance), adassana (non-vision), and anabhisamaya (non-realization)—are merely synonyms (vevacana) for one another. In this Saṃyutta, it should be understood that eleven discourses and fifty-five expositions (veyyākaraṇa) are taught.

The Commentary on the Vacchagotta Saṃyutta is finished.

## 13. Jhānasaṃyuttaṃ

## 1. Samādhimūlakasamāpattisuttavaṇṇanā

In the first discourse of the Jhāna Saṃyutta, 'samādhikusalo' (skilled in concentration) refers to one who is skilled in defining the factors of jhāna, such as the first jhāna having five factors and the second jhāna having three factors. 'Na samādhismiṃ samāpattikusalo' (not skilled in attainment regarding concentration) refers to one who is unable to attain jhāna after having gladdened the mind and made it ready. In this manner, the meaning of the remaining terms should also be understood.

## 2-55. Samādhimūlakaṭhitisuttādivaṇṇanā

663-716. In the second discourse and others, 'na samādhismiṃ ṭhitikusalo' (not skilled in steadiness regarding concentration) refers to one who is unskilled in maintaining the jhāna, being unable to keep the jhāna steady for even the duration of seven or eight finger-snaps. 'Na samādhismiṃ vuṭṭhānakusalo' (not skilled in emerging from concentration) refers to one who is unskilled in emerging from jhāna, being unable to emerge at the predetermined time. 'Na samādhismiṃ kallitakusalo' (not skilled in readiness regarding concentration) refers to one who is unskilled in gladdening the mind and making it ready for attainment. 'Na samādhismiṃ ārammaṇakusalo' (not skilled in the object of concentration) refers to one who is unskilled in knowing which specific object among the kasiṇa objects is suitable for them. 'Na samādhismiṃ gocarakusalo' (not skilled in the resort of concentration) refers to one who is unskilled and lacks mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the 'resort' (gocara) of meditation subjects as well as the 'resort' village for alms. 'Na samādhismiṃ abhinīhārakusalo' (not skilled in resolution regarding concentration) refers to one who is unskilled in specially directing the meditation subject as a suitable practice. 'Na samādhismiṃ sakkaccakārī' means one who does not habitually act with respect and care in attaining jhāna. 'Na samādhismiṃ sātaccakārī' means one who does not habitually act with perseverance in attaining jhāna, but only does so occasionally. 'Na samādhismiṃ sappāyakārī' means one who is unable to fulfill the helpful states (appanā-kicca) that are suitable for concentration. After that, with terms such as attainment (samāpatti)...
324:
By combining with the terms, the tetrads (catukka) are taught. The meaning of those tetrads should be understood in the manner already stated. In this entire Jhāna Saṃyutta, everything is taught by way of the teaching, specifically by way of mundane jhāna (lokiyajjhāna).
